articles.title: I turned my GitHub contribution graph into a Bloomberg-style trading terminal
articles.description: TL;DR: Your green contribution squares are a heatmap. I wanted a chart. So I built...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR: Your green contribution squares are a heatmap. I wanted a chart.
So I built gh-trading-terminal: a GitHub Action that renders your real contribution calendar as a TradingView / Bloomberg-style terminal, as one self-contained SVG you drop into your profile README.

🔗 Repo: hanzlabaig-dev/gh-trading-terminal (MIT, Node 18.3+, 0 dependencies)


The preview uses synthetic sample data. Yours uses your real contribution calendar.

🧭 What's inside the terminal

Every panel is plain SVG, and you choose which ones to show:

Panel What it draws show name
🕯️ Candlesticks One daily candle per day, with a pulsing candle for the current UTC day (always on)
🔊 Volume Raw contributions per day under the chart volume
📊 Analytics 10 stats: total, avg/day, active days, current and longest streak, best day, volatility (σ), Sharpe, max drawdown, best weekday stats
🟩 Heatmap Last 26 weeks, weekday × week heatmap
📈 Weekly volume Last 12 weeks, with week-over-week change weekly
🗓️ Monthly close Last 6 months, with month-over-month change monthly
🧾 Ticker tape A scrolling strip of your key numbers tape
〰️ SMA A 20-period moving average line sma
🌫️ Bands A ±2σ band around the same 20-period window bands

Everything is on by default except bands (use show: all to turn it on).

💡 The header also shows your Developer Index, a fictional 0 to 1000 score, with a sparkline and a pulsing LIVE dot.

⚡ Setup in 3 steps (no server, no hosting)

Step 1: Add a workflow

In your profile repo (USERNAME/USERNAME), create .github/workflows/terminal.yml:

name: Update trading terminal
on:
  schedule: [{ cron: '17 */6 * * *' }]
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  terminal:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hanzlabaig-dev/gh-trading-terminal@v1
        with:
          days: 90
          theme: tradingview
          token: ${{ secrets.GH_PAT || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

Step 2: Run it once

Go to the Actions tab → Update trading terminal → Run workflow.
It renders and commits two files:

  • assets/terminal-dark.svg
  • assets/terminal-light.svg

Step 3: Embed it in your profile README.md

This <picture> block follows the viewer's light/dark theme:

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" srcset="assets/terminal-light.svg">
  <img src="assets/terminal-dark.svg" width="100%" alt="GitHub contribution trading terminal">
</picture>

🔒 Want your private contributions included?
  1. Create a token with the read:user scope.
  2. Save it as the repo secret GH_PAT.
  3. Enable "Private contributions" in your GitHub profile settings.

If the default token is rejected, use GH_PAT. That's why the workflow reads secrets.GH_PAT || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN.

🎛️ Action inputs

input default notes
username repo owner any GitHub login
days 90 14 to 730
theme / light-theme tradingview / light tradingview, bloomberg, midnight, light
output-dir assets where the SVGs are written
show all but bands stats,heatmap,weekly,monthly,volume,tape,sma,bands or all
extra-args (empty) any CLI flag, e.g. --colorblind true --hide tape --up #00ff88
commit true set false to handle commits yourself

🎨 The four themes
Theme Look
tradingview the default dark theme (navy background, teal/red candles)
bloomberg amber text on pure black, green/red candles
midnight GitHub-dark style palette
light the default for terminal-light.svg

♿ Colorblind mode and custom colors

Colorblind mode swaps the candle colors to blue (up) and orange (down):

- uses: hanzlabaig-dev/gh-trading-terminal@v1
  with:
    extra-args: "--colorblind true --hide tape --up #00ff88"

⚠️ Quote the extra-args value. In YAML, an unquoted # starts a comment, so --up #00ff88 would silently get cut off.

Color flags: --up, --down, --bg. The smoothing factor is --alpha (default 0.5, clamped to 0.1 to 0.9).


🧮 How the numbers work

GitHub only exposes daily contribution totals, so real intraday OHLC data does not exist.
Instead, candles are a deterministic mapping of your real counts. Nothing is fabricated.

The "price" is an exponential moving average (EMA) of your daily activity:

level(t) = level(t-1) + alpha * (count(t) - level(t-1))

From that level, each candle is built like this:

open  = level(t-1)
close = level(t)
high  = max(open, close, count(t), count(t-1))
low   = min(open, close, count(t), count(t-1))
  • 🟢 green when close >= open (the day beat the running level)
  • 🔴 red otherwise

A few details I like:

  • Volume is the raw count per day. Huge spikes are clipped to a sensible axis limit and marked with a small triangle, so one monster day can't flatten the whole chart.
  • An empty in-progress day does not break your current streak yet. The day isn't over.
  • The current UTC day is drawn as a pulsing, translucent candle, because that session is still open.

The Developer Index (0 to 1000)

A rolling 28-day blend of four components. It's fictional, but fully reproducible:

Component Weight How it's computed
Active-day ratio 35% share of days in the window with at least 1 contribution
Intensity 25% log(1 + mean) / log(1 + 10), capped at 1
Streak 20% current streak ÷ 14 days, capped at 1
Stability 20% 1 - min(1, stdDev / mean / 3)

Two more stats complete the picture:

  • Sharpe = mean ÷ standard deviation of your daily counts
  • Max drawdown = the worst peak-to-trough fall of the Developer Index

⚠️ It's a joke index with real math behind it. Not financial advice, and not a performance review either.

🧱 The constraint that shaped everything

GitHub serves README images through an image proxy that blocks scripts, CSS and web fonts. So the SVG is built to survive that:

  • ✅ plain SVG attributes only (no <style>, no scripts, no external references)
  • ✅ a system monospace font stack
  • ✅ SMIL for all animation: the pulsing candle, the LIVE dot and the scrolling tape
  • ✅ works in any <img> tag
  • ✅ self-contained: about 38 KB at 90 days, and still under about 100 KB at the 730-day maximum

The test suite even enforces it: every theme is rendered and asserted to contain no <script>, <style>, <foreignObject> or external URLs.

Other things worth knowing:

  • GraphQL allows under a year per query, so longer ranges are chunked automatically (360-day chunks, de-duplicated by date).
  • GitHub caches images, so changes can take a few minutes to show. The SVG prints its own UPDATED time.
  • Commits made by the Action bot don't count as your contributions. (No infinite-green-squares exploit, sorry.)

🛠️ Other ways to run it

CLI (Node 18.3+, zero dependencies):

git clone https://github.com/hanzlabaig-dev/gh-trading-terminal && cd gh-trading-terminal
npm test
npm run demo        # synthetic data, no token needed
GITHUB_TOKEN=xxx node src/cli.js --user YOU --from 2026-01-01 --to 2026-11-22 --theme bloomberg --out terminal.svg

🚩 All CLI flags 
--user --days --from --to --theme --show --hide
--animate false --colorblind true
--up --down --bg --alpha --demo --out

Live URL (optional): deploy to Vercel, set GITHUB_TOKEN, and use this as the image URL (served by api/terminal.js, cached for 1 hour):

https://YOUR-APP.vercel.app/api/terminal?user=YOU&theme=bloomberg&days=120

✅ Tested

npm test runs 6 tests with Node's built-in test runner. They cover candle invariants, streak logic, rendering every theme safely, display toggles and input validation, the chunked GraphQL fetch, and the Action's entrypoint script. CI runs them on Node 18, 20 and 22.

🤝 Contributing

PRs are welcome, and the layout is easy to navigate:

You want to add... Look in
a new theme src/themes.js
layout changes src/render.js
new metrics src/analytics.js

Run npm test before opening a PR.

🎬 Try it

  1. ⭐ Star the repo: hanzlabaig-dev/gh-trading-terminal
  2. Drop the workflow into your profile repo
  3. Tell me in the comments: what's your Developer Index? 📈

Which panel or metric should I add next? Let me know below. 👇

articles.title: Monuments of India, Part 4: 100 New Monuments, from Harappan Dholavira to the Chenab Rail Bridge
articles.description: In Part 3 the work was about depth: sixteen statues sculpted again from photographs, a rebuilt Mysore...
articles.body_html:
In Part 3 the work was about depth: sixteen statues sculpted again from photographs, a rebuilt Mysore Palace and an 800k triangle budget. In the comments someone asked what the goal of the project is. My answer was to add as many of India's structures as possible, so the styles of each period and region can be studied side by side.

This post is about that breadth. Monuments of India has gone from 101 monuments to 201. Every one of the 100 new ones is built the same way as the first 101: in three.js, from code, with no downloaded 3D models.

Here is the round of work in short:

  1. Three batches: 24 temples, stations, airports and bridges; 26 ASI sites and three modern landmarks; then 50 more covering faiths, periods and regions that were missing.
  2. Every state: the map now covers 35 states and union territories, up from 26. All 28 states are in, and every union territory except Lakshadweep.
  3. More of India's faiths: five gurdwaras, seven churches, five mosques, two synagogues, a Parsi fire temple and a Tibetan monastery, beside the temples.
  4. Older and newer: from the Harappan cities of Dholavira and Lothal (c. 3000 BCE) to the New Pamban Bridge (2025).
  5. New shared parts: trains, platforms, airliners and jet bridges; gurdwara domes and the Nishan Sahib; Kerala ring roofs, wagon-vault roofs, a Meitei roof and more, written once and reused.

The pictures below are the plain studio views from the project's own screenshot scripts. The live site adds shadows, photo textures and haze.

The numbers

Before Now
Monuments 101 201
States and union territories 26 35
Lines of monument code added about 8,800

By kind, the 100 new monuments are 55 sacred buildings, 21 civic works (stations, bridges, stepwells, an observatory, a launch pad), 18 forts and palaces, and 6 memorials. Karnataka gained the most (11), then Tamil Nadu (9), Maharashtra (8) and Gujarat (7).

Nine states and territories appear for the first time: Tripura, Chhattisgarh, Haryana, Mizoram, Manipur, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Puducherry, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.

How a new monument is added

Each batch went through the same steps, and each step was its own commit, so the site never broke in between.

  1. Register: an entry in js/data.js with the place, dates, style, material, a headline figure and three facts for the plaque, plus a placeholder builder. The map can show it before the model exists.
  2. Filters: every monument must fall into at least one style group and one material group in the sidebar, and tools/check-filters.mjs fails if one doesn't. The new monuments needed new patterns: Kashmiri, Maratha wada, Bundela, Art Deco, Harappan, Parsi, Meitei, Khasi and Kalachuri.
  3. Build: drafts of the whole batch first, then finished in groups of four or five, each checked against photographs and published plans.
  4. Pictures: the gallery and the state-by-state list are regenerated.
  5. Share: anything one monument needed that another could use was moved out of the monument and into the shared kit, and documented with a picture.

Step 2 is why some regexes in js/filters.js have grown long. This is the "Regional & mixed" group now:

// Styles of their own: Sikh, the Himalayan pagoda, Keladi forts, the Gommateshwara monolith, the
// brick temples of Bengal, Ahom Assam, Ladakh's palace, the Karkota temples of Kashmir, the
// Maratha wada, the Bundela palaces, the Harappan cities, the Parsi fire temple, Meitei Manipur,
// the Khasi root bridges, Elephanta, and the buildings that mix several traditions.
{ id: 'regional', label: 'Regional & mixed',
  test: /sikh|pagoda|keladi|monolithic|mixed|bengal|ahom|ladakhi|kashmiri|maratha wada|bundela|harappan|assyrian|meitei|khasi|kalachuri/i },

Batch one: temples, stations, airports and bridges (101 to 125)

The first 24 filled gaps in the famous temples and, for the first time, added India's railways, airports and space programme.

Temples: Lingaraja, the Sun Temple at Modhera with its stepped tank, Dwarkadhish, Badrinath, the Bishnupur terracotta temples, Dakshineswar Kali Temple, Bhoramdeo and Virupaksha at Hampi.

Railways and airports: Howrah Station, Chennai Central, Charbagh Station in Lucknow, Mumbai Airport Terminal 2 and Bengaluru Airport Terminal 2. These needed things the kit had never had, so a new js/parts/transport.js was written before any of them:

  • track(): ballast, concrete sleepers every 0.65 m (1.3 m on phones) and two rails at broad gauge.
  • train(): coaches on bogies with a locomotive, in the liveries of Indian trains: ICF blue, red LHB Rajdhani, green, suburban EMU, and Vande Bharat with a raked nose at each end.
  • overhead(): masts, cantilevers and the catenary and contact wires at 5.5 m.
  • platform(): an island platform under a butterfly canopy on iron columns.
  • airliner(): an A320 or a 787 in outline, with any tail colour.
  • jetBridge(): a boarding bridge from a rotunda to its cab, on a wheeled leg.

Placing a train on a bridge is then two lines, as on the New Pamban Bridge:

g.add(at(track(2 * HALF + 60, { ballast: false }), 0, RAIL_Y - 0.42, TRACK_Z));
f.add(at(train(detail.low ? 9 : 12, { livery: 'blue', locoColour: '#b8402f' }), -28, RAIL_Y + 0.1, TRACK_Z));

Bridges: the Chenab Rail Bridge, the highest railway bridge in the world, with its deck 359 m above the river and a steel arch of 467 m across the gorge. The deck runs straight and then curves to the Kauri end, as the real one does. The New Pamban Bridge is 99 spans of plate girders and one 72.5 m lift span between two towers, with a train crossing.

The launch pad: the Satish Dhawan Space Centre is the Second Launch Pad with an LVM3 on it, as for Chandrayaan-3: the rocket on its mobile pedestal over the flame trench, the umbilical tower, four lightning masts, and the twin track to the Vehicle Assembly Building. That building is about a kilometre away in fact; here it is brought in to 300 m so it fits the view.

The rest:

  • Jantar Mantar, Jaipur: every gnomon's edge is set at Jaipur's latitude, 27° above the north horizon, so it points at the celestial pole as the real instruments do. The Vrihat Samrat Yantra is 27 m high.
  • Chand Baori: about 3,500 steps down 13 storeys. A pit can't be cut out of a flat ground plane cheaply, so the land round it is modelled as raised blocks whose tops are the ground, and the well goes down between them. The Modhera tank uses the same trick.
  • Matrimandir: a flattened golden sphere 36 m across, set with about 1,400 gilded discs, among twelve petals of red stone.
  • Statue of Equality: Ramanuja seated on a lotus, 216 ft in all. It was later corrected against a photograph: dhoti folds, a slimmer build, a smile, a leaning staff with its flag, beads and earrings.
  • Rang Ghar in Assam, Ujjayanta Palace in Tripura, Leh Palace, and the Vidhana Soudha in Bengaluru.

Batch two: ASI sites and three modern landmarks (125 to 151)

The second batch was mostly sites protected by the Archaeological Survey of India that the first 101 had missed, plus Prem Mandir in Vrindavan, ISKCON Bangalore and Adiyogi.

Temples: the Pancha Rathas at Mamallapuram, five shrines each cut whole from one granite outcrop as a model of a different kind of temple: a thatched hut, a small vimana, a barrel-roofed hall, a three-storey vimana and an apsidal shrine, with the elephant, lion and Nandi beside them. Also Airavatesvara at Darasuram, Lepakshi with its 8.2 m monolithic Nandi, the Pattadakal group, Mukteswara, Martand Sun Temple in Kashmir, Jageshwar, the Laxman Temple at Sirpur (brick), and the unfinished Bhojeshwar Temple with its 2.3 m linga.

Forts and palaces: Kumbhalgarh with part of its 36 km wall, Kangra Fort, Warangal Fort with its Kakatiya toranas, Purana Qila, Shaniwar Wada, Jahaz Mahal at Mandu, Jahangir Mahal at Orchha, the Lotus Mahal at Hampi, Mattancherry Palace in Kochi, and Hazarduari Palace, the palace of a thousand doors (a hundred of them false). Talatal Ghar in Assam shows its four storeys above ground; the three below ground aren't drawn.

Others: Sheikh Chilli's Tomb in Haryana with its pear-shaped dome, Sé Cathedral in Old Goa, and the Vikramshila Mahavihara, a cruciform Pala brick stupa faced with rows of terracotta plaques.

Adiyogi is the one statue in this round, and it got the same treatment as the statues in Part 3. It was rebuilt twice from photographs taken from the front, both sides, below and behind: a bust 45 m across with shoulders sloping to the ground, thick ropes of hair running from the crown to the ground, the ears left bare, the cobra standing on the right shoulder, the eyes fully closed and the third eye a tall white flame. In front are the terrace and the pavilion of the Yogeshwar linga. Adiyogi joined the monuments with large statues that may build to a million triangles on desktops.

Batch three: fifty more (151 to 201)

The last batch was chosen to fill what was still missing: faiths, the oldest periods, the north-east and the smaller union territories.

Gurdwaras, churches, mosques, synagogues and a fire temple

  • Gurdwaras: Takht Sri Hazur Sahib, Takht Sri Patna Sahib, Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib, Gurudwara Bangla Sahib, and Hemkund Sahib at about 4,630 m, on a star-shaped plan built to bear the snow. With the Akal Takht already in the Golden Temple's model, four of the five Takhts are now on the map; only Damdama Sahib is still to come.
  • Churches: St Paul's Cathedral in Kolkata, San Thome Basilica, Christ Church Shimla, the Church of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception in Panaji, St Francis Church in Kochi, and Solomon's Temple in Aizawl, a white marble hall 120 ft square with a crowned tower at each corner.
  • Mosques: Taj-ul-Masajid, Mecca Masjid, Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra, Cheraman Juma Masjid and Sidi Saiyyed Mosque with its Tree of Life jali.
  • Synagogues: the Paradesi Synagogue in Kochi and the blue Knesseth Eliyahoo in Mumbai.
  • Fire temple: the Wadiaji Atash Behram in Mumbai, with bull-capital columns after Persepolis and the Faravahar.
  • Monastery: Namdroling at Bylakuppe, with its gilded roofs.

The five gurdwaras share a new js/parts/sikh.js: the ribbed gilt onion dome in its lotus cup under a gilt umbrella, the Nishan Sahib with its saffron pennant and khanda, storeys of arcaded faces, and rows of small gilt domes along the parapets.

The oldest sites

  • Dholavira, the Harappan city in the Rann of Kutch, from the excavated plan: the castle on its high mound with battered stone sides, the bailey, the ceremonial ground, the middle and lower towns, and the reservoirs cut into the rock. The real city is about 771 by 617 m; it's drawn at a little under half so the whole fits the view.
  • Lothal, the Harappan port, with its brick dock 214 by 36 m.
  • The Barabar Caves, the oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India, with the Lomas Rishi doorway carved as a wooden hut: the earliest chaitya arch.
  • The Ashokan Pillar at Vaishali, the Great Chaitya at Karla with its teak ribs, and the Elephanta Caves with the Trimurti.

Temples, stepwells and the Sultanates

  • Temples: Gangaikonda Cholapuram, the Kailasanathar Temple at Kanchipuram with its ring of 58 small shrines, the twin Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebidu, the apsidal Durga Temple at Aihole, Teli ka Mandir with its wagon-vault roof, Vadakkunnathan in Thrissur, the Masrur rock-cut temples and the Bateshwar group.
  • Stepwells: Adalaj and Agrasen ki Baoli.
  • Sultanate and Deccan: Tughlaqabad Fort, the Mahmud Gawan Madrasa, Ibrahim Rauza and Bara Gumbad.

Colonial and modern

The Viceregal Lodge in Shimla, Eros Cinema (the project's first Art Deco building), Umaid Bhawan Palace, Louis Kahn's IIM Ahmedabad, and Falaknuma Palace.

The north-east and the union territories

  • Kangla Fort in Imphal, with the two white Kangla Sha, guardian beasts with a lion's body and a dragon's head, 5.9 m high, before the ruined coronation hall.
  • The double-decker living root bridge at Nongriat in Meghalaya. This one has no stone at all: each deck is a bundle of roots drawn as tubes that wander and braid round the deck's line, thicker near the banks where they spring from the fig trees, with railings of roots tied down by hanging roots.
  • The Kohima War Cemetery in Nagaland, Moti Daman Fort, and the Aayi Mandapam in Puducherry.

New parts in the shared kit

Once the batches were built, everything reusable was moved out of the monuments and into the shared parts, the same rule as in Parts 2 and 3. Every model stayed the same after the move, except one: the Wadiaji Atash Behram's column shafts had been sitting half a storey below their capitals, and now reach them.

  • Temples: the Kerala ring roof and gopuram, the chandrashala and gavaksha (the horseshoe window motif), the wagon-vault roof, spire canopies, a broken spire for ruined towers, apsidal plans, and the Kakatiya thorana.
  • Doorways: the Lomas Rishi and Mauryan doorways.
  • Roofs and ornament: gable, lean-to and Meitei roofs, the Tree of Life jali, pierced walls, the Faravahar, stepped merlons and the trishul.
  • Colonial: a Gothic turret and a tower clock.
  • Mughal: the pear-shaped dome.
  • Forts: the battered wall and the arrowhead bastion.
  • Figures: the Kangla Sha, the Ashokan pillar, elephant and bull columns, and the Trimurti.
  • Gurdwaras and railways and aircraft, as above.

The components page has a picture of every one, and the guides have moved into docs/, with pointer pages left at the old paths so existing links still work.

The budget, still

Doubling the number of monuments didn't change the rules. Every monument is built at two levels and checked by the budget checker: 800,000 triangles on desktops and 300,000 on phones. The monuments with large sculpted statues, now twelve with Adiyogi, may go to 1,000,000 on desktops, because a face and hands meshed finely are where the triangles show.

Because each monument's code is loaded only when it's opened, the map still comes up without fetching 201 models first. One practical change came with the larger gallery: the screenshots alone were about 69 MB per deployment, so a .vercelignore now keeps screenshots, docs and tools out of what gets deployed.

Also in this round

Since Part 3, alongside the new monuments, some older ones were corrected against photographs:

  • The Red Fort's front and the Capitol Complex in Chandigarh rebuilt.
  • Mysore Palace's side fronts, its gate and grounds, and the two-tier central dome.
  • Laxmi Vilas Palace shortened by a quarter to its real 155 m, with the tower raised to 60 m.
  • Shivaji at the Gateway of India with a full beard, open eyes and fingers round the sword's hilt, and Patel's and Netaji's faces given closer likenesses.

What's next

The project now covers all 28 states and every union territory but one. The next steps are the same two as before: add what's still missing (Lakshadweep is the obvious gap), and take the photograph-by-photograph pass that the statues and Mysore Palace got to the buildings that are still closer to massing models.

If you like the project, a ⭐ on the GitHub repo helps other people find it. Contributions are welcome too: a new monument, or a correction to one you know well.

Further reading in the repo:

  • monuments.md: all 201 monuments, state by state, with a picture of each
  • components.md: every shared part and statue
  • architecture.md: the parts, by tradition
  • how-it-is-drawn.md: budgets, loading and the desktop and phone differences

Which monument from your state is still missing? Tell me in the comments.

articles.description: I'm a 53-year-old self-taught developer with no formal degree. 😂  Last year, my mobile game was...
articles.body_html:
I'm a 53-year-old self-taught developer with no formal degree. 😂

Last year, my mobile game was rejected by the Play Store. Not because of the code: I simply couldn't find enough testers to meet the store requirements, and I got stuck. It drove me crazy, and it would have been easy to give up.

This year, after many late nights and a complete pivot towards BeeLadybug, I finally won my personal challenge against the Chrome Web Store. It's officially live, and for me, this is a huge milestone.

I won't turn this into a long self-promotion post, so I'll keep it short: BeeLadybug (v1.0.5) is a free, open-source Manifest V3 Chrome extension that analyzes the layout and CSS issues of the page you're viewing and lets you download an HTML report.

If you want to try it out, poke around the code, or even suggest improvements, here are the links:

  • 🧩 Chrome Web Store: Install BeeLadybug
  • 💻 Source Code: GitHub Repository
  • 📄 Sample report: See what the extension exports
  • 🎮 Live demo of the core library: BeeLadybug CanvasAdapter demo

If you're a self-taught dev or you've ever been blocked by app store policies, I'd love to hear your story in the comments. Thanks for reading! 🐝

articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

What I Built

I built FocusPulse, an empathetic, contactless bio-adaptive co-pilot designed for neurodivergent individuals managing ADHD.

People with ADHD struggle daily with sustained attention, hyperfocus burnout, sensory overload, and autonomic task paralysis (a physiological fight-or-flight freeze state). Traditional tools often fail because they require manual tracking or intrusive smartwatches—demanding effort and adding tactile discomfort.

FocusPulse turns any standard webcam into a real-time neuro-physiological monitor. It non-invasively tracks rPPG cardiac vitals, respiratory motion, eye aspect ratios, and head kinematics to detect autonomic stress and mind-wandering before the user consciously experiences burnout. Instead of blaring alarms, FocusPulse responds with non-punitive micro-interventions: peripheral 40Hz focus beats, screen dimming, micro-task chunking, and vagal breathing biofeedback.

Snip about my project

Demo

  • Live Production App: https://focuspulse-760833501708.us-central1.run.app/
  • Dual Operation Modes:
    1. Live Webcam rPPG Mode: Click "Enable Camera rPPG" to stream contactless vitals in real time.
    2. Simulated SmartSpectra Engine: Test all ADHD state triggers instantly without a camera using the built-in scenario switcher.

Code

  • Public Repository: https://github.com/AravindFLASH/adhd-google

Setup Instructions 

# Clone the repository
git clone [https://github.com/AravindFLASH/adhd-google.git](https://github.com/AravindFLASH/adhd-google.git)
cd adhd-google

# Run the local server
node server.js

Open http://localhost:3000 in Chrome or Edge, click "Enable Camera rPPG", and grant camera permissions.

Key Features

  1. Live webcam rPPG metrics: pulse, HRV (RMSSD), stress index
  2. Dual respiration tracking: thoracic vs abdominal patterns with TAR mode detection
  3. Eye and gaze layer: blink rate, stare duration, adaptive eye pointer overlays
  4. Motion-energy detection: separates still focus from restless behavior
  5. Bio-adaptive interventions:
  6. Paced breathing orb
  7. Focus pulse cues
  8. Micro-task paralysis buster
  9. Optional smartwatch BLE bridge
  10. Live-only telemetry cards so users see real camera data only

How It Responds to Human Signals
The Presage SmartSpectra SDK extracts clinical-grade physiological signals without skin contact by analyzing micro-vascular capillary blood volume flushes and optical flow from ordinary consumer webcams.

                        [ Webcam 30 FPS Video ]
                                   │
                                   ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

articles.body_html:
A translation can look polished and still be dangerous to apply. The application may preserve the words while quietly losing the most useful review artifact: what the person actually wrote.

Consider a synthetic event brief: “Please keep Room 204 available until Friday. The budget is $250. Do not confirm the booking until Maya approves.” The room, amount, deadline, and condition all matter. A translation belongs beside that source so someone can inspect the result before using it.

This walkthrough builds a safer interaction in React and TypeScript with Chrome’s Language Detector and Translator APIs. The companion lab includes a manual source-language selector, an availability check for the selected pair, cancellation, stale-result protection, and a separate acceptance action. It never submits a booking or sends the brief to a cloud model.

Separate detection from the translation decision

Language detection returns candidates. A short message, a proper name, or mixed-language text may not provide enough evidence for a reliable automatic choice. Display the leading candidates and let the person confirm the source language.

Do not treat the detector’s confidence as a score for the eventual translation. These are different operations with different failure modes. A confident identification of English says nothing about whether a particular translation preserves a conditional deadline.

The interface uses two actions: Detect language, then Translate on this device. That separation also gives translation a fresh user interaction when model preparation requires it.

Figure 1. Detection informs the language choice. Acceptance remains a separate application action.

Check the requested pair before the click

Feature detection answers whether an API is exposed. Availability answers a more specific question about the requested operation.

if (typeof Translator === "undefined") {
  setAvailable("Translator API is not exposed here.");
} else {
  Translator.availability({
    sourceLanguage: source,
    targetLanguage: target,
  }).then(
    value => setAvailable(`Selected pair: ${value}.`),
    () => setAvailable("Availability check failed.")
  );
}

Run this probe when the language selection changes. In the full React component, an effect cleanup prevents an older probe from updating the label after a newer selection. A slow probe changes the label to “Readiness is still unknown”; a timeout does not prove that the API is unsupported.

An unavailable feature should leave the editor useful. Keep the source text editable and offer manual copying. Do not silently turn a local translation action into a server request.

Chrome’s current documentation describes these APIs on desktop and notes that language-pack availability reporting protects information about previously used pairs. Consequently, an availability label should guide preparation rather than become a detailed inventory of the person’s installed languages.

Create the translator from the action

The adapter receives the exact source text and language pair. It owns one translator and releases it after use.

async function translateText(
  text: string,
  sourceLanguage: string,
  targetLanguage: string,
  signal: AbortSignal
) {
  signal.throwIfAborted();
  const translator = await Translator.create({
    sourceLanguage, targetLanguage, signal,
  });
  try {
    return await translator.translate(text, { signal });
  } finally {
    translator.destroy();
  }
}

Call this directly from the translation handler. Avoid placing an unrelated asynchronous operation before creation and assuming transient user activation will still exist afterward. The lab performs its readiness probe separately and catches creation errors in the handler.

The complete adapter also checks for missing APIs and empty input and reports download progress. Progress describes preparation; it is not an estimate of translation accuracy or remaining generation time.

Keep the result attached to its source

While translation runs, the person might change “Friday” to “Thursday” or select another language. The earlier response must not appear as a translation of the new text.

The lab invalidates the pending request whenever the source text or either language changes. A request identity check prevents a late response from becoming current even if cancellation does not immediately stop the underlying work. A completed suggestion is cleared by the same changes.

This is especially important at acceptance time. A button that applies an old suggestion after the original has changed can undo the person’s latest work. Keep the acceptance handler tied to the current suggestion, and invalidate it as soon as its inputs change.

Rendering the suggestion as ordinary React text keeps it from becoming executable HTML. If the product later adds Markdown, its rendering policy needs a separate review.

Test the interaction and the language quality separately

The companion’s deterministic tests cover superseding and cancelling requests. Those checks establish which result may be displayed; they cannot establish whether the translation reads naturally or preserves meaning.

Use a small review set before calling the feature useful:

Input case What to inspect
Room number and budget Identifiers and amounts remain correct
“Do not confirm until approved” Negation and prerequisite remain intact
Short ambiguous phrase Manual source selection remains available
Mixed languages Candidate uncertainty is visible
Unsupported pair Original remains editable; no cloud request occurs
Source edited during generation Old output cannot become the current suggestion

Ask a fluent reviewer to compare the original and translation. A reverse translation can reveal something worth investigating, but it is not an independent ground truth and can repeat the first model’s mistake.

Run the companion

From the supplied lab directory, run npm ci and npm run dev. Open the printed localhost address in a compatible browser. The native action buttons use real browser APIs; they do not return canned translations when support is missing.

The code is typechecked against the pinned Chromium AI declarations. Translation quality still requires a native model run and language review; no accuracy percentage is claimed here. Record the browser version, language pair, input, and actual output when conducting that review.

A useful translation feature lets someone recover from uncertainty without losing the message they meant to send. Which parts of your application’s user-written text must survive translation exactly, and which need a human judgment about meaning?

References

  • Chrome Translator API
  • Chrome Language Detector API
  • Design AI user experiences
  • Evaluation-driven development

articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

What I Built

Every music teacher has said it: “You stopped breathing in bar 12.”

Pianists, guitarists, string players and drummers hold their breath through hard passages all the time, and almost never notice.
That breath hold brings stiff shoulders, a rushed tempo and fumbled notes, and it gets much worse when the recording light comes on.
You can’t watch yourself breathe while you’re reading a score. A webcam can, and with SmartSpectra it can tell you which bar.

Breathmark is a desktop practice companion (Electron + SmartSpectra):

  1. Set up a piece. Enter the tempo, time signature, number of bars, and sections such as rehearsal marks (A · Opening, B · Hard run, …). No sheet music needed.
  2. Settle (30 s). Sit how you’ll play and breathe normally. Breathmark records your resting breathing activity and pulse for today.
  3. Play against the built-in metronome. A big bar counter, beat dots and a scrolling chest-movement trace drawn on the bar grid keep you oriented.
  4. Get a bar map. Your run comes back as something that looks like a score: every bar is colored from breathing freely to guarded to held. A breath mark (’) appears above the bar line where you should breathe, for example “Breathe before bar 10. You held 4.9 s through bars 10–11.”
  5. Come back tomorrow. Each section gets a trend across runs: still bracing → loosening up → body knows it. Bars that keep needing a breath mark get flagged.

Your fingers can learn a passage days before your body stops bracing for it. Breathmark makes that second kind of learning visible.

Two extras I’m especially happy with:

  • Red-light mode. It simulates recording pressure: a blinking REC light, a take number, and no click after the count-in. It then compares your tension with your normal practice runs (“Under recording pressure your breath tension is 1.5× your practice runs, and your pulse peaks +12 bpm higher.”). Nothing is actually recorded.
  • A gentle cue. After about 4 seconds of held breath during practice, a soft “’ breathe” glows at the edge of the screen. It’s optional, and it’s always off in red-light mode.

Demo

1. A real SmartSpectra run, no simulation

The real SDK running inside the app: API key, piece setup, the SDK’s framing hints, a 30-second settle baseline from real pulse and breathing, the live chest-breathing trace on the bar grid, and the report.
A short CC BY test clip stands in for the webcam (face blurred on screen; the SDK sees the full frames).

2. The full tour (Demo mode)

A 2½-minute captioned walkthrough on simulated signals, so you can see a breath hold on cue: the hard passage, the “’ breathe” cue, breath marks, progress across days, and red-light mode.

Video 1 test clip: by Fury ARA (YouTube), licensed CC BY 3.0, via the Internet Archive. Used unmodified as camera input; blurred on screen.




No key? No camera? Click Add demo piece → Load sample history (or Demo run). Everything runs on clearly labelled simulated signals, so you can explore the whole app in two minutes.

Code

Aryakoste / Breathmark

’ Breathmark

Find the bars where you stop breathing.

Breathmark is a practice-room companion for musicians. You play a piece against its metronome while your webcam watches you. Using the Presage SmartSpectra SDK, it maps every bar where you held your breath or your pulse climbed onto a score-like bar map. It then suggests where to pencil in a breath mark (’).

Play the piece again tomorrow and Breathmark shows which passages your body has learned and which it still braces for, even after your fingers know the notes.

Why

Teachers say “keep breathing!” about hard passages all the time. Pianists, guitarists, string players and drummers routinely hold their breath through tricky runs without noticing That tension stiffens the shoulders, rushes the tempo and gets much worse under performance pressure (“red-light fever” when the recording light comes on) You can’t watch yourself breathe while you read music. A camera…

View on GitHub

npm install && npm start. Paste your Presage API key in Settings & privacy, or use Demo mode. Requires Node 20+ on Windows x64, macOS Apple Silicon or Linux.

How It Responds to Human Signals

Breathmark requests breathingMetrics + cardioMetrics through the SDK’s Electron renderer integration (bindSmartSpectraIpc in main, the SDK preload, and the renderer SmartSpectraSDK).

Lining up the body with the bar grid. The WebAudio metronome schedules clicks with a look-ahead scheduler and reports the epoch time at which bar 1 / beat 1 sounds.
SmartSpectra timestamps every measurement in epoch microseconds, so each chest-trace sample maps onto an exact bar and beat.

Breath holds from breathing.upperTrace. I first tried a rolling standard deviation of the chest trace, and it failed in an instructive way: a 2.5-second window that happens to sit on the top of a breath looks “still”.
Breathmark now measures breathing activity as the chest’s mean absolute speed over 2.5 s, as a ratio to your settle baseline. That has three advantages:

  • it doesn’t depend on where in the breath cycle the window falls;
  • it ignores slow posture drift;
  • it reads near zero during a hold at any chest level. Players often freeze half-way through an inhale, which an amplitude-around-the-mean measure misses.

Below 30 % of rest for 3.5 s or more counts as a hold, and below 55 % as guarded. Shorter pauses, like the natural one at the end of an exhale, are ignored.
Unit tests check that a 7-second hold lands on the right bar, that a mid-inhale freeze is caught, and that slow (8/min) and fast (20/min) breathing never trigger false holds.

Pulse from cardio.pulseRate. The SDK reports a 12-second rolling average, so Breathmark shifts it back 6 s to line up with the bars that caused it. It then reports each section’s pulse relative to your resting pulse, not as an absolute number.

Signal quality from validationStatus. The status is turned into friendly framing hints (“Tilt the camera so your shoulders and upper chest are visible”).
The settle countdown pauses while the signal isn’t usable. Bars where the SDK can’t see you (no face, chest not visible, too dark or too bright) are shown hatched as no data and are never counted as “calm”. Testing against the real SDK taught me one more thing: it keeps streaming the chest trace through motion warnings, and musicians move while they play. So Breathmark keeps those samples. Motion can only make a hold look like breathing, never the reverse, so the worst case is a missed breath mark, never a false one.

Prize Categories

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use. It answers a real, everyday question that musicians and teachers already ask (“where am I tensing up?”), and it turns the answer into something a musician already uses: a breath mark pencilled into the score.

Most Creative or Delightful Use. The output is a score, not a dashboard. Red-light mode turns a performance-anxiety cliché into a practice tool.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Camera consent. A first-run consent screen explains everything below and must be accepted. The camera turns on only when you press Start camera in a session and turns off when you leave it. Electron is configured to grant only video (never the microphone), and only to the app’s own local page.
  • Video is processed on-device by the SmartSpectra SDK. Breathmark never stores, records or uploads video or images. Red-light mode only simulates recording.
  • Stored locally only. Pieces and runs (per-bar scores, a 10 Hz chest trace, pulse estimates and the settle baseline) live only in the app’s local storage on your computer. There is no Breathmark server, account or analytics. Each piece keeps its latest 30 runs.
  • Delete and export. Delete single runs or pieces, or use Settings → Delete everything (data, saved key and consent). Export all (JSON) gives you your data, with the API key redacted.
  • API key. It is held in memory by default. An opt-in “remember” stores it unencrypted locally, and the UI says so. The SDK sends it to Presage for authentication.
  • SDK telemetry is off by default (enableTelemetry: false). If you turn it on, the SDK sends session summaries (SDK version, OS and device, frame and quality statistics, coarse errors) to Presage. These are linked to the API key, never include video or vitals values, and the Settings page explains this.
  • No AI services are used (no requestInsight, no LLM calls).
  • Not medical. It is a practice and wellness aid with no diagnosis, treatment or clinical claims. It is designed for measuring yourself with the camera in plain view, never for monitoring other people.

This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

What I Built

TraderZen is an autonomous, contactless biometric desktop companion and cognitive circuit breaker for financial traders, powered by the Presage SmartSpectra SDK.
When trading volatile markets (crypto, forex, equities, or prop firm challenges), the biggest threat to capital isn't the market—it’s "Tilt" (emotional revenge-trading, adrenaline rushes, and despair-fueled sizing). Traders ignore passive desktop notifications during fight-or-flight states.
TraderZen solves this by floating unobtrusively alongside your charting terminal (TradingView, MetaTrader, etc.), continuously analyzing your physiological and affective state using standard webcam feeds. When your biometric thresholds are breached (e.g., heart rate > 95 BPM, hyperventilation, or an acute spike in anger/fear > 70%), TraderZen triggers an Executive Tilt Circuit Breaker:

  • Full-Screen Optical Blur: It instantly frosts your entire screen in heavy 40px backdrop blur, making your order book and broker physically untouchable.
  • Audio-Guided Box Breathing: A circular breathing pacer guides you through a 4-second box-breathing cycle (Inhale → Hold → Exhale → Hold) with soothing acoustic harmonics.
  • Autonomic Recovery Lock: Your desktop remains protected until your physiological vitals return below risk thresholds, complete with a deliberate 3-second hold-to-override safeguard so the trader always retains final agency.

Demo

Demo Video: https://youtu.be/120ZZGrQzg8

Key Screenshots:

Code

  • Repository: https://github.com/Abhinandangithub01/Trader_Zen
  • Tech Stack: Electron, Node.js, Presage SmartSpectra SDK (@smartspectra/node-sdk v3.5.0), C++ Native FFI (smartspectra_capi.dll), Web Audio API, esbuild.

Setup Instructions 

git clone https://github.com/Abhinandangithub01/Trader_Zen.git
cd Trader_Zen
npm install
npm start

How It Responds to Human Signals

TraderZen integrates 9 simultaneous Presage SmartSpectra biometric modalities in real time via the native MediaPipe C++ pipeline:

  1. Cardio Pulse Rate (MetricType.PULSE_RATE): Sub-frame rPPG facial chrominance processing computes live Heart Rate (BPM). An animated heart icon beats synchronously with physical heart contractions.
  2. Respiration Cadence (MetricType.BREATHING_RATE, CHEST_BREATHING): Monitors chest wall displacement and breathing frequency to detect rapid shallow breathing and hyperventilation during market volatility.
  3. Facial Affect & Emotion Classifier (MetricType.EXPRESSIONS): Decodes protobuf expression scores to classify 8 affective states (ANGRY, FEAR, HAPPY, NEUTRAL, SAD, SURPRISE, CONTEMPT, DISGUST). If confidence in ANGRY or FEAR exceeds 70%, it immediately trips the Emotional Rage Lock.
  4. Verbal Agitation & Outbursts (MetricType.TALKING): Monitors jaw movement and vocalization status, flagging shouted distress or heavy exasperated sighs at the screen.
  5. Eye Blink Cadence & Fatigue (MetricType.BLINKING): A 60-second rolling window monitors blink frequency. If blinks drop below 7/min, the HUD displays a DROWSY / FATIGUE alert for late-night session traders.
  6. 468-Point 3D Face Mesh & Head Posture (MetricType.FACE_LANDMARKS): Tracks 3D coordinate displacement (x, y, z) between the forehead, nose tip, and chin. It detects when a trader buries their face in their hands or slumps forward in despair.
  7. Chair Micro-Motion Restlessness (GLUTES_MICROMOTION, KNEES_MICROMOTION): Measures sub-millimeter physiological tremors and vibration in the chair, flagging impatient leg-bouncing and motor restlessness.
  8. Compound Tilt Risk Index: Aggregates all human signals into a unified 0–100 autonomic risk score:
    • Baseline Heart Rate over resting ceiling (up to 50 pts)
    • Respiration hyperventilation penalty (up to 20 pts)
    • Hostility & panic affect (Anger/Fear > 40% adds up to 30 pts)
    • Verbal agitation outburst (+15 pts)
    • Chair restlessness jitter (+10 pts) Classifies state into Optimal (Green), Elevated (Amber), or Critical Tilt (Rose/Red).

SmartSpectra SDK Integration Walkthrough

We connected Electron's renderer with the native C++ FFI bridge using sdk.useMediaStream(stream) and protobuf decoding:

  • 30.0 FPS Monotonic Timestamp Ratchet: Standard USB 2.0 webcams frequently jitter between 24 and 29 FPS under auto-exposure. We implemented an epoch timestamp anchor (timestamp.js) guaranteeing strict 33,333 µs intervals, preventing graph starvation errors.
  • Automated Graceful Recovery: Replaced fatal pause states with an automated debounce recovery handler (sdk.reset() followed by in-place sdk.start()), ensuring the sensor re-arms seamlessly if video focus changes.

Prize Categories

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use

  • Real-World Need: Emotional discipline is the #1 reason 90%+ of retail traders and prop firm candidates fail. During sudden market drawdowns, the sympathetic nervous system triggers fight-or-flight adrenaline rushes, causing traders to double down, move stop-losses, or revenge-trade their accounts to zero.
  • Who It's For: Day traders, crypto scalpers, prop firm challenge participants (FTMO, Topstep), and high-stress computer knowledge workers.
  • Thoughtful Design:
    • Passive desktop notifications are consistently ignored during acute tilt; TraderZen physically locks the display behind an unclickable frosted glass barrier to force a mandatory biological cool-down.
    • It respects trader agency: a 3-second hold-to-override prevents impulsive bypasses while ensuring a user can still exit an emergency position if needed.

Most Creative or Delightful Use

  • Rather than building another passive dashboard or mock trading exchange, TraderZen turns contactless webcam signals into a proactive, physical guardian of your financial capital.
  • Features dynamic acoustic entrainment tones (Web Audio API) matched to physiological states and real-time box breathing pacers. ## Consent and Data Handling
  • Camera Consent: TraderZen accesses the webcam strictly with the user's explicit browser/OS permission prompt via navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia. A visible, high-definition camera viewport with alignment reticles is always shown so the user is fully aware when sensing is active.
  • 100% Local On-Device Processing: Video frames never leave the host machine. All computer vision and rPPG extraction calculations are performed entirely on-device by the native C++ smartspectra_capi engine.
  • Zero Video Storage or Transmission: Raw camera frames and facial images are discarded immediately after in-memory buffer processing; zero frames are written to disk, uploaded to the cloud, or transmitted over the network.
  • Telemetry: Remote telemetry is explicitly disabled (enableTelemetry: false). User configuration rules are stored strictly on the local machine via localStorage.
  • Non-Medical Disclaimer: TraderZen is an autonomic biofeedback performance and discipline tool for trading; it is not a medical device and makes no claims to diagnose, treat, or monitor clinical health conditions.

articles.description: A mental model for organizing styles in design systems, starting with the native capabilities of the web platform and progressively building toward more complex abstractions.
articles.body_html:
When exploring different approaches to organizing styles in design systems, I've noticed that we often lean heavily on class names while overlooking some of the native building blocks already provided by the web platform and the browser.

I have found it really helpful to approach styling through a clear, step-by-step hierarchy, moving naturally from foundational concepts all the way up to complex components. The idea is to start with what the browser already gives us for free, then progressively layer on what we must define ourselves.

I call this approach TEACH. It's an easy-to-remember mental model that helps me organize styles in a progressive order of complexity and foundational importance:

  • Tokens
  • Elements
  • Attributes
  • Classes
  • Hgh-level components

Focusing on these layers in this order can help build cleaner style libraries. By leaning on everything the browser and web platform already offer first, we can create more robust systems before writing custom high-level components.

Layered approaches to CSS architecture aren't new. Harry Roberts' ITCSS organizes styles into layers, moving from generic, low-specificity rules to more explicit, higher-specificity ones. TEACH is my way of organizing the building blocks involved in styling a design system into a single, easy-to-remember order.

Tokens

Tokens are the foundation of the style library. They are custom properties that define the core values of the system, from fonts and colors, to spacing and border radii.

Any customizable value that would be reused should have a token. Reusability is the key part there. We want to have consistent theming that is easy to update and facilitates white labeling.

Some classic examples for tokenization are colors; we may want a primary brand color, a secondary color, and perhaps tertiary or accent colors that are shared across buttons, headings, links, borders, and more.

:root {
  --primary-color: #36c;
  --secondary-color: #444;
  --accent-danger: #d22;
  --text-primary-color: #fff;
  --spacing-0: 0;
  --spacing-1: 0.25rem;
  --spacing-2: 0.5rem;
  /* ... */
}

The number of tokens will likely shift while developing the design system as more needs emerge. Do not fear changes at this stage, but be thorough: this is the foundation for everything that follows.

Finding the sweet spot for tokenization is tricky, and it varies from team to team and project to project. I like to view it much like database normalization: too little, and you end up with repetition and redundancy; too much, and you find yourself splitting hairs over tokens that are rarely ever reused.

Elements

Native HTML elements are often overlooked in favor of classes, but in my opinion, they are an essential layer that should be front and center in any style library.

I like to treat this layer as an opinionated normalizer: different browsers apply different default styles to native elements. Use element selectors to normalize those differences while applying basic, library-oriented styles driven by the tokens.

a {
  color: var(--primary-color);
  text-decoration: underline;
  /* ... */
}

button {
  background: var(--primary-color);
  border: 1px solid transparent;
  color: var(--text-primary-color);
  display: inline-block;
  padding: var(--spacing-2);
  /* ... */
}

An obvious advantage of this approach is achieving a more unified experience across browsers. But there is another major benefit that should not be overlooked: as soon as the library is imported into a project, the pages instantly adopt the library's look and feel, without changing any class names or adding extra markup.

At this point, we have built the core of the style library without introducing any custom classes. There are many examples of classless libraries out there. Pico CSS is a great example: a lightweight CSS framework that shows how much you can do by styling native elements directly, with no extra classes required. (I even built a classless library myself!)

We have a foundation that harnesses all of HTML's built-in semantic and accessibility powers before scaling up further. That is the true beauty of TEACH: it is designed to be semantic, accessible, and scalable at its core.

While native HTML is generally accessible out-of-the-box, it is easy to break that by applying the wrong CSS styles. Never underestimate the power of CSS to break accessibility if mismanaged.

Attributes

Take advantage of the built-in platform features whenever possible:

  • HTML includes many native attributes that can provide semantic information and serve as styling hooks.
  • ARIA states and roles can provide accessibility-related information that can also be used as styling hooks.
  • CSS pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements can target specific states or parts of an element.

Focusing on native features reduces and simplifies code while also helping shift the team's mindset toward clearer, more usable, more semantic, and more accessible patterns.

For example, we could style a custom combo button using a class like .combo-button-menu-expanded, or we could use the aria-expanded HTML attribute alongside the [aria-expanded="true"] CSS selector. The former is fine for humans, but the latter benefits both humans and machines by communicating explicit state information through the browser's accessibility APIs, making it available to assistive technologies. Not to mention, in some cases, this strategy avoids human error by keeping styles automatically in sync with the actual DOM state.

Stop for a second and think, "Do I need a class for this, or is there a native alternative already built in?" Consider some common native patterns:

  • Instead of .accordion-open, use [open],
  • Instead of .input-is-invalid, use :user-invalid,
  • Instead of .checkbox-switch, use [role="switch"],
  • Instead of .menu-expanded, use [aria-expanded="true"]...

Note: This does not mean we should use ARIA attributes and roles for everything instead of classes. Misusing ARIA can lead to frustrating experiences for assistive technology users. Rely on native semantic tags and attributes first, use ARIA when it genuinely fits the case, and fall back to classes when in doubt.

At this stage, we still haven't defined a single custom class or component in our style library, yet we've already established a cohesive look-and-feel and leveraged native elements and attributes to style and communicate dynamic states.

Classes

Classes are the fourth layer of this five-layer hierarchy. This placement is not meant to diminish their importance (they are a core pillar of any style library). Rather, it reflects my preference for using classes as an extension mechanism when the underlying HTML and CSS features aren't sufficient. Not the default.

A classic example for using classes is styling anchor links to look like buttons, a common pattern found in most websites. By sharing styles across element selectors and utility classes, we ensure consistent design without repeating code:

button,
.btn-primary {
  background: var(--primary-color);
  border: 1px solid transparent;
  color: var(--text-primary-color);
  display: inline-block;
  padding: var(--spacing-2);
  /* ... */
}

Pure CSS components find their home in this layer. Components such as a layout grid system, flex containers, or utility wrappers. These patterns organize layout rather than style a specific semantic tag or component. Classes provide the ideal mechanism to apply them across the markup.

This eventually leads to a philosophical crossroads: should something be a class or an attribute? Should it be <button class="btn-primary"> or <button data-variant="primary">?

This is not a debate of classes vs. native attributes. This section is about classes and data attributes. Which approach works best for your project in terms of readability, usability, and maintenance is ultimately up to your team to decide.

High-Level Components

High-level components, or simply components (TEACH worked better as an acronym than TEACC), are where the style library stops being just a collection of styles and matures into a true UI architecture. Tokens, elements, attributes, and classes have already done the heavy lifting; this final layer packages everything into reusable, encapsulated building blocks.

A component is typically a custom element or a framework component. A self-contained piece of UI that bundles its own structure, styles, and behavior. I place them at the very top of the TEACH hierarchy because they should build upon the layers below them.

Components are where the design system becomes more portable and easier to adopt. Product teams can simply drop in a <date-picker> or a <user-card> without having to worry about low-level implementation details.

These components still require their own styles, but because we did the work effectively in the previous layers, that custom CSS is considerably reduced. In many cases, we could lean entirely on our underlying native elements and attributes to handle core states and functionality. It is a win-win.

user-card {
  background: var(--secondary-color);
  margin: var(--spacing-2);
  padding: var(--spacing-3);
  /* ... */
}

If we are using web components, these elements may rely on the shadow DOM for encapsulation. Even though it isolates styles from the rest of the page, the TEACH hierarchy would still be a great guide for structuring what goes inside them.

The styling for these components can be implemented in a thousand different ways: vanilla CSS, Tailwind, Sass, or CSS-in-JS... all while continuing to follow the TEACH mental model.

Conclusion

When looking at many design systems, I often see a strong emphasis on design tokens and high-level components, with native HTML elements and attributes treated almost as an afterthought.

There's nothing wrong with that approach, but it reminds me of the classic demonstration of filling a glass jar. If you only pack it with big rocks, you end up with a lot of empty space. You need the smaller gravel and sand to fill the gaps. That is precisely where the Elements and Attributes in TEACH fit in.

This model is not meant to replace what you are already doing. Instead, it offers a complementary mental shift: a way to pursue simplicity and functionality across every layer of web architecture.

  • Tokens
  • Elements (native)
  • Attributes (native)
  • Classes
  • High-level components

While I like this mental model, I know it isn't a one-size-fits-all method for every project or architecture. It may not fit particularly well with a utility-class-first approach, and globally scoped element selectors will make some design system architects cry foul.

This is simply my preference, and I know it won't work for everyone. Take the parts that make sense for your project, adapt them to your needs, or use them as inspiration for your own approach. Whatever direction you choose, make sure to teach your style library to make the most of the semantic, styling, and accessibility features already provided by the web platform.
