Spider Paint capability not limited to serve my VR program, fare beyond that it is capable functional as a browser based 3D engine which can creat, handle and explore a larger scene also. I cannot tell the secret when I told this is also completly fine for any interactive 3D game development also, build and play in one program.

Welcome to Wyoming, a space station in my Five Percent universe, with the Seventh Quadrant spacecraft docked alongside it.

What you're looking at is not a rendered movie. It's a live scene running inside my own browser-based 3D engine, 3Draft.

The station and the ship were assembled in a surprisingly simple way: almost like LEGO. Using MCP, I built the environment from modular, low-poly pieces. Even the sixty-four characters scattered around this world were created with a reusable human-modeling module.

For this demonstration, I've removed the outer walls. That means we can see directly into the different floors, rooms, corridors, and connected structures without constantly fighting the camera.

Now watch how I move through the scene.

I can orbit around a selected target, slide sideways using parallax scrolling, or switch to another target and travel straight towards it. There is no special camera path prepared for this video. I'm simply navigating the world as it runs.

In fact, this is the same basic navigation logic I use when travelling between stars. The scale is completely different, of course, and the spacecraft controls are more sophisticated, but the underlying idea is the same: choose a destination, move through space, and explore.

As we approach the Seventh Quadrant, the large station becomes a collection of smaller, more personal spaces. An airlock, a corridor, a crew member standing under the lights. Suddenly, it feels less like a 3D model and more like a place you could visit.

And there's another important detail here.

I've deliberately switched off the normal lighting. Almost everything you can still see comes from emissive materials: glowing floor strips, signs, panels, screens, and small architectural accents.

These simple light sources give the low-poly environment a surprisingly convincing nighttime mood, without having to fill the whole station with elaborate visual effects.

Finally, we reach the Dockside Bar. It's a small scene within a much larger world, but I can move from one to the other without changing engines or changing navigation systems.

That's what I wanted to demonstrate.

3Draft isn't just about creating objects. It's about putting those objects together into large, interactive spaces, and making them easy to explore.

Vibe first. Explain later.

articles.title: Netlify Isn't Just a Static CDN: How Atomic Deploys, Edge Isolates, and Content-Addressed Storage Actually Work Under the Hood
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute deep dive into Netlify architecture. Learn how content-addressed trees eliminate cache invalidation, how atomic pointer flips guarantee zero asset drift, why Deno V8 edge isolates start in 5ms, and how the Smart CDN routes requests without central bottlenecks.
articles.body_html:
Ask most developers what Netlify is, and you will hear a familiar, casual summary:

"It is a wrapper around AWS S3 and CloudFront with automated git push webhooks."

It is an understandable assumption. In the early days of the web, publishing a website meant opening an FTP client like FileZilla and uploading files directly to an Apache server. Later, cloud infrastructure refined this workflow: you configured an AWS S3 bucket, set up a GitHub Action, ran aws s3 sync dist/ s3://my-bucket/, and issued a CloudFront cache invalidation.

If you have ever managed that pipeline in production, you have also experienced the silent nightmare it creates: The Asset Drift Trap.

Imagine a user browsing your site during an active deployment. The S3 sync script begins uploading files alphabetically. The browser navigates to a new page, requesting index.html. It receives the newly deployed HTML, which points to main.a8f2c.js. But the deployment script has only uploaded up to the letter C; main.a8f2c.js does not exist in S3 yet.

The user's browser throws a fatal error: HTTP 404: ChunkLoadError. The user stares at a blank white screen until they clear their cache.

Traditional file-hosting systems treat files as mutable physical objects resting in folders. When you upload a new version, you overwrite the previous version. If an upload fails halfway through, your site is broken. If an update introduces a catastrophic bug, rolling back means recompiling and re-uploading every file from scratch.

Netlify solved this fundamental flaw by throwing away traditional file hosting entirely.

Netlify is not an S3 sync script. It is an immutable, distributed database modeled on Git tree cryptography, combined with content-addressed storage, zero-second atomic pointer switches, and Deno V8 edge isolates.

Here is what actually happens under the hood when you push code to Netlify.

1. The Build Container: From Git Webhook to Content-Addressed Tree

When you type git push origin main, GitHub dispatches an HTTPS webhook payload to Netlify's build scheduler.

Within milliseconds, Netlify provisions an isolated Linux build container. This environment runs your configured build command (e.g., npm run build or vite build), compiling your source code into a directory of static assets (dist or build).

In traditional hosting, the build runner would immediately start uploading those files over HTTP by path name (/index.html, /assets/app.js).

Netlify does something entirely different: it content-hashes every file.

The SHA-256 Content-Addressing Pass

Before transferring any data over the network, the build agent calculates the cryptographic SHA-256 digest of every file's raw binary contents:

dist/index.html        ──► sha256 ──► 8a3f12c...
dist/assets/app.js     ──► sha256 ──► d41d8cd...
dist/assets/logo.svg   ──► sha256 ──► 9e107d9...

Notice that the hash depends strictly on the file's binary contents, not its file name or path.

The build agent constructs a JSON data structure called the Deploy Manifest Tree. This manifest maps relative web paths to their corresponding SHA-256 hashes:

{
  "/index.html": "8a3f12c5b8e919...",
  "/assets/app.js": "d41d8cd98f00b2...",
  "/assets/logo.svg": "9e107d9d372bb6..."
}

The Delta Upload

Next, the build agent sends this manifest to the Netlify Deploy API.

Netlify queries its global content-addressed blob store and asks a simple question: Which of these hashes do we already possess?

If you have a site with 1,000 files, and your latest commit only altered two CSS classes in main.css, 998 of those files will produce identical SHA-256 digests to the previous deployment.

Netlify replies with a list containing only the missing hashes:

{
  "missing": [
    "8a3f12c5b8e919...",
    "d41d8cd98f00b2..."
  ]
}

The build container uploads only those two missing binary blobs. The remaining 998 files are never transferred over the wire. They already exist in Netlify's global storage pool from previous builds.

This delta upload mechanism is why Netlify deploys frequently complete in two to three seconds, even for massive static repositories.

2. The Atomic Deploy Switch and Instant Rollbacks

Once all missing blobs are stored, Netlify creates a new immutable record: deploy_id = dep_64f1a92e.

At this exact moment, your new site version is completely uploaded, yet zero production traffic has touched it.

The Atomic Pointer Flip

In traditional hosting systems, deployments are gradual. Files are overwritten in place over several seconds or minutes, creating dirty states where old HTML references missing new JavaScript bundles.

Netlify guarantees atomicity.

Across Netlify's global edge network, every incoming HTTP request resolves your domain name (example.com) to a specific deploy_id pointer.

To publish a build, Netlify executes an atomic pointer update:

[ example.com ] ──► (Pointer) ──► [ dep_64f1a92e (New Manifest) ]
                                  [ dep_52a8c110 (Old Manifest) ]

This pointer switch takes zero milliseconds.

One microsecond, a request hits dep_old; the next microsecond, a request hits dep_new. There is never an intermediate phase where some files belong to the old version and some belong to the new version.

The Magic of Zero-Second Rollbacks

Every developer has experienced that sinking feeling when a production release breaks user authentication or corrupts checkout forms.

In traditional architectures, rolling back requires checking out the previous git commit, spinning up a CI runner, rebuilding the project, and waiting ten minutes for a deployment pipeline to complete.

In Netlify, rolling back does not involve building or uploading.

Because every previous deployment was content-addressed and saved as an immutable manifest tree, the old files still exist in the global blob store. When you click Rollback to this deploy in the Netlify dashboard, Netlify simply repoints your domain pointer back to the previous deploy_id:

[ example.com ] ──► (Pointer Repointed) ──► [ dep_52a8c110 (Previous Manifest) ]

The rollback executes instantaneously worldwide. Zero rebuilding. Zero downtime. Zero risk.

Isolated Preview Deployments

This architecture also explains why Netlify can provide unlimited Deploy Previews (deploy-preview-42--mysite.netlify.app) and branch subdomains for every pull request at zero marginal storage cost.

Each pull request creates its own manifest tree. Because the underlying blobs are deduplicated across the entire account, storing fifty concurrent branch previews consumes almost no extra disk space compared to storing a single deployment.

3. Inside the Smart CDN: Invalidation-Free Caching

Traditional Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) were designed for static assets like images and videos. They struggle with modern web applications because HTML files change constantly.

To keep websites fresh, traditional CDNs rely on Cache Invalidation APIs (PURGE /*). When you deploy, your CI server asks the CDN to wipe its cache across hundreds of edge locations.

Cache purging has three notorious drawbacks:

  1. Slow Propagation: Wiping thousands of worldwide edge caches takes between thirty seconds and fifteen minutes.
  2. Thundering Herd Problem: When an edge node wipes its cache, the next wave of visitor requests slams your origin server simultaneously, spiking CPU and database load.
  3. Cache Inconsistency: Edge nodes in London might receive the purge signal five minutes before edge nodes in Singapore, leading to regional behavior discrepancies.

Netlify designed its Smart CDN (an Anycast edge mesh) to eliminate cache invalidations completely.

How Edge Request Resolution Works

When a user in London visits example.com/about:

  1. Anycast DNS Routing: The request routes through Anycast BGP to the geographically nearest Point of Presence (PoP) in London.
  2. Local Memory Manifest Lookup: Every edge server maintains a lightweight, in-memory key-value map of active site pointers and manifest trees.
  3. URL Resolution: The edge node reads the manifest for example.com at the current deploy_id. It maps /about to its cryptographic hash: sha256:7f3a8b....
  4. Cache Hit: If the edge node already holds the binary blob for sha256:7f3a8b... in its local SSD or NVMe cache, it streams the response immediately.
  5. Cache Miss & Origin Shield: If the edge node does not have the blob, it requests it from Netlify's Origin Shield, caches it locally, and serves the user.

Why Netlify Never Needs Cache Purging

Because every asset in the manifest tree is identified by its cryptographic SHA-256 hash, assets are fundamentally immutable.

If app.js changes, its hash changes. The new deploy manifest points /assets/app.js to a brand-new hash.

The edge node never needs to delete the old app.js from its cache. It simply stops resolving incoming requests to the old hash. If an active user is still holding an open browser tab from the previous deployment, their browser can continue fetching the old asset hash without error, while new visitors immediately receive the new asset hash.

This allows Netlify to set the most aggressive caching headers possible for static assets:

Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

The browser can cache the asset locally for an entire year with zero risk of stale data.

4. Edge Functions vs Serverless Functions: The V8 Isolate Advantage

Modern web applications are rarely pure static files. They require authentication checks, personalized dashboards, A/B testing, and dynamic server-side rendering (SSR).

Netlify provides two distinct execution engines for compute: Serverless Functions and Edge Functions.

Understanding the architectural difference between them is critical for building low-latency applications.

Serverless Functions (AWS Lambda Under the Hood)

Standard Netlify Functions (placed in netlify/functions/) run on top of AWS Lambda.

When a request arrives for a serverless function:

  1. If the function is cold, AWS allocates a Firecracker micro-virtual machine.
  2. It spins up a Linux user space, boots a Node.js or Go runtime, and imports your application dependencies (node_modules).
  3. This boot process creates a Cold Start Latency of 200ms to 800ms.
  4. The function executes in a single centralized cloud region (e.g., us-east-1). If a user in Sydney makes a request, the packet must cross the Pacific Ocean to Virginia, wait for execution, and travel back.

Serverless functions excel at complex transactions: querying relational databases, processing payments with Stripe, generating PDF invoices, or executing background jobs with up to 15-minute timeouts.

Edge Functions (Deno & V8 Isolates)

Netlify Edge Functions (placed in netlify/edge-functions/) run directly on the CDN edge nodes using V8 Isolates powered by Deno.

A V8 Isolate is not a container, virtual machine, or separate operating system process. It is an isolated JavaScript execution context within a single, continuously running C++ process.

Because an isolate requires no OS bootup or runtime instantiation:

  • Cold Starts are Sub-5 Milliseconds: An isolate can spin up, execute, and terminate in less time than a single TCP packet takes to traverse the network.
  • Global Proximity: Edge functions execute on the exact edge node nearest to the user (in Tokyo, Frankfurt, or São Paulo).
  • Direct Response Streaming: Edge functions can intercept incoming HTTP requests, inspect cookies, rewrite headers, or transform the response HTML stream using the native Web Streams API before the bytes leave the edge server.

Use Edge Functions for:

  • Geolocation detection (redirecting / to /de/ for German users).
  • A/B testing without layout shift (serving variation B directly from the edge without client-side JavaScript flashes).
  • JWT authentication verification before proxying to origin.
  • Dynamic OpenGraph image generation.

5. The Edge Routing Engine: Demystifying _redirects

At the heart of every Netlify deployment is its edge proxy routing engine, configured through the _redirects file or netlify.toml.

Many developers view _redirects as a simple URL rewriter. In reality, it is a high-performance reverse proxy that executes directly in the edge network's request pipeline.

The engine evaluates rules top-to-bottom. The first rule that matches an incoming path executes.

Rule 1: The SPA Fallback (Status 200 Rewrite)

Single Page Applications built with React, Vue, or Svelte handle routing client-side via the browser History API. If a user directly enters example.com/dashboard/settings, the server must return index.html with an HTTP 200 status while preserving the URL path in the browser address bar:

# netlify/_redirects
/*    /index.html   200

This is not a redirect; it is an internal edge rewrite. The browser URL does not change, search engines do not register a 301 hop, and the client-side router takes over upon load.

Rule 2: Micro-Frontend Reverse Proxying (Status 200!)

Modern enterprise architectures frequently split monolithic web applications into specialized micro-frontends or separate backend APIs:

# Proxy API requests to an external Kubernetes cluster
/api/*  https://api.internal-corp.com/:splat  200!

When an external request hits example.com/api/v1/users:

  1. Netlify's edge node opens an outbound streaming connection to https://api.internal-corp.com/v1/users.
  2. It proxies the payload directly to the client.
  3. The client browser believes it is talking to example.com.

This technique completely eliminates Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) preflight OPTIONS requests, reducing API request latency by an entire round trip.

Notice the exclamation mark: 200!.

By default, Netlify uses shadowing: if a real static file exists at /api/v1/users.json in your build output, Netlify serves that file and ignores the rewrite rule. Adding the exclamation mark (200!) forces the rule, ensuring the reverse proxy always triggers even if a static file matches.

Rule 3: Geo-Targeting and Role-Based Access at the Edge

Netlify allows you to inject edge metadata directly into your routing table without writing custom backend code:

# Serve localized marketing page for visitors in Great Britain
/   /uk/home   302   Country=gb

# Protect admin dashboard using Netlify Identity roles
/admin/*   /login   401!   Role=admin

Because these rules are evaluated directly in the edge node's request cycle, unauthenticated users or unauthorized regions are blocked before a single byte of application code executes.

6. Production Traps: Hard Lessons from the Edge

Building on an atomic edge architecture introduces distinct operational patterns. Avoiding these three common traps will save your team hours of debugging:

Trap 1: The Multi-Repo Asset Drift Trap

While Netlify guarantees atomic deployments within a single repository, teams adopting micro-frontends often deploy header, navigation, and core application modules from separate repositories.

If the navigation repository updates its global CSS classes while the application repository has not deployed its updated markup, visual regressions occur.

When designing micro-frontends across separate Netlify sites, always pin shared component libraries to immutable semver versions rather than pointing to latest branches.

Trap 2: Unbounded Edge Function Proxy Loops

Because Edge Functions can rewrite URLs, and rewrite rules can trigger Edge Functions, careless routing configurations can trigger infinite edge loops:

// Edge function intercepting /api
export default async (request: Request, context: Context) => {
  // If this rewrite triggers the same edge function again:
  return context.rewrite("/api/processed");
};

If /api/processed also matches the edge function's path pattern, the edge node will cycle recursively until it hits Netlify's internal loop threshold (returning HTTP 500: Subrequest loop limit reached).

Always ensure that rewritten paths bypass edge function matcher patterns using explicit exclusion paths in netlify.toml:

[[edge_functions]]
function = "auth-check"
path = "/api/*"
excluded_paths = ["/api/public/*", "/api/processed/*"]

Trap 3: Memory Exhaustion in Edge Isolates

V8 isolates are blazingly fast because they share an operating system process, but they operate under strict resource ceilings.

A Netlify Edge Function typically enforces a 50ms CPU execution limit and a 128MB memory ceiling.

If your edge function attempts to parse a 40MB JSON payload or uses heavy regex evaluations on large strings, the isolate will be abruptly terminated by the edge supervisor (Isolate CPU limit exceeded).

Keep edge functions lightweight. Use them for routing decisions, cookie validation, and streaming transformations. Offload heavy computation and bulk data crunching to standard Serverless Functions or background workers.

The Mental Shift

The evolution from traditional file servers to Netlify represents a broader philosophical shift in software architecture:

The web is no longer composed of files sitting on servers.

The modern web is a content-addressed graph of immutable binary blobs, coordinated by cryptographic hashes, governed by atomic pointers, and enhanced by V8 compute isolates running at the edge.

When you understand this architecture:

  • You stop worrying about cache invalidation because deploys are immutable.
  • You stop fearing production releases because rollbacks are instantaneous.
  • You eliminate asset drift because user sessions are locked to consistent manifest trees.
  • You design faster applications by placing lightweight compute within five milliseconds of your users.

How has the transition to atomic deployments and edge routing shaped your team's release velocity? Have you replaced legacy backend reverse proxies with edge rules or migrated heavy Lambdas to V8 Isolates? Share your production experiences and architecture patterns in the comments below.

articles.body_html:
An Ancient Idea in a Digital World

It's 1:30 a.m.

The café is still open, although only a few lights above the counter are on.

I'm wiping down the coffee machine when the little bell above the door rings.

A young man walks in with a laptop bag over his shoulder. His eyes look tired, and he looks like he's had a very long day.

"Are you still open?"

"You're in luck. You look like you need a coffee more than I do."

He laughs.

"I've just finished a deployment. Things are stable for now. I need a coffee. Something strong."

"For now?"

"Anyone working in IT knows what that means. You never know what's coming next."

I make him an espresso.

"Sounds like you've had a day full of changes."

"Don't get me started. Requirements change, technologies change, teams change. Sometimes I just wish the whole world would pause for a moment."

I slide the coffee across the counter.

"There's an old book on my shelf that might have something to say about that."

He follows my finger and looks at the bookshelf.

"The I Ching?"

"That's the one."

"I've heard of it. Isn't it some kind of fortune-telling book?"

"That's what a lot of people associate it with. But there's something else about it that I find more interesting."

"What's that?"

"Change."

He takes a sip.

"People were studying change thousands of years ago?"

"More seriously than you might think."

An Old Book, Two Lines

I take the old book from the shelf and grab a paper napkin.

On it, I draw one solid horizontal line, then another line with a gap in the middle.

"These are called Yang and Yin lines in the I Ching."

He looks at them.

"Two lines?"

"That's right. For the sake of our little conversation, you can think of the Yang line as 1 and the Yin line as 0."

His expression changes.

"Hold on. Zero and one?"

"What about them?"

"Isn't that just binary? The foundation of computing?"

I smile.

"Programmers. You see two lines and immediately think of binary."

"Well, can you blame me? What else can you do with them?"

"Add another line."

Eight Trigrams on a Napkin

I draw a few combinations of three lines on another napkin.

"Three lines can be combined in eight different ways. These are the Eight Trigrams."

I write a few numbers beside the drawings:

000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110, 111.

We read each trigram from the bottom line upward.

He stares at the numbers, picks up his phone, and taps a few buttons.

"Two to the power of three. Eight!"

"Exactly."

"Tell me something. What about six lines?"

"Sixty-four."

I write on the edge of the napkin:

2⁶ = 64

He studies it for a moment, then laughs.

"You're turning the I Ching into a binary tutorial."

"I'm just using a language you're more familiar with."

The Interesting Part Is the Change

He takes another sip of coffee.

"So the sixty-four hexagrams are just sixty-four fixed patterns?"

I shake my head.

"That would be missing the interesting part."

"Why?"

I pick up the pen and change one of the lines in a hexagram.

"Because the lines can change. A Yin line can become Yang, and a Yang line can become Yin. When a line changes, the whole hexagram may become something else."

He watches the little drawing.

"So the point isn't just to remember what it is, but to see what it might become?"

"More or less. You also have to look at why it's changing."

He leans back in his chair. For the first time tonight, he seems genuinely interested in something other than his deployment.

"That's a bit like working with systems. Something can look fine when it goes live, but that doesn't mean it'll stay that way. More users, more data, changing business needs... suddenly the architecture that worked yesterday doesn't quite fit anymore."

"Mmm."

"Teams are the same. Development, testing, product, infrastructure. They all affect one another. A change in one place means the others have to adjust, too."

I look at his cup.

"You haven't even finished your coffee, and you've already started talking about work again."

He laughs.

"Occupational hazard. Can't help it."

It Also Depends on Where You Stand

I take away his empty espresso cup and set a fresh glass of water beside him.

"There's another interesting detail in the I Ching."

"Go on."

"Besides looking at whether a line is Yin or Yang, you also look at where it sits."

"Where it sits?"

"The same Yang line can mean something different depending on its position. The same goes for a Yin line."

"Some positions are considered suitable for Yang, others for Yin."

He thinks for a moment.

"So it's not just about whether someone has the ability to do something. It's also about whether they're in the right position?"

"Not a bad way to put it."

"Sounds a bit like organizational management again."

"Looks like tonight's coffee wasn't wasted."

In a six-line hexagram, the positions are counted from the bottom up. The first, third, and fifth positions are Yang positions. The second, fourth, and sixth are Yin positions. A Yang line in a Yang position, or a Yin line in a Yin position, is generally considered to be in its proper place.

He picks up his water glass, only to discover that it's empty again.

"So, what exactly is dynamic balance?"

Balance Doesn't Mean Standing Still

I'm about to answer when the coffee machine makes a little warning sound.

I turn to deal with it. When I come back, he's still staring at the napkin.

"Well, balance doesn't necessarily mean both sides are equal. And it certainly doesn't mean everything has to stand still."

"Then what does it mean?"

"Most of the sixty-four hexagrams describe a kind of balance that's still moving. A few are special cases, but the interesting thing is how the situation keeps changing."

"Sometimes one side grows while the other recedes. Sometimes a situation changes, the old balance is lost, and a new one gradually takes shape."

He nods.

"So balance itself keeps changing."

"Now you're getting somewhere."

He suddenly laughs.

"You know, I only came here tonight for a coffee. I didn't expect to end up studying ancient Chinese philosophy."

"That happens."

"Really?"

"Late-night cafés have a way of bringing out conversations that might never happen during the day."

He glances at his laptop, then back at the napkin.

"Next time, you'll have to tell me about all sixty-four hexagrams."

I collect his empty glass.

"Sure."

"Really?"

"Of course."

"Great!"

"But that's enough for tonight."

"Why?"

"You've had enough philosophy for one night, and I need a break, too."

He laughs.

"So there's a cover charge for the philosophy?"

"Naturally. Did you think I could explain several thousand years of ideas over a single cup?"

We both laugh.

He folds the napkin and slips it into his laptop bag.

Just before leaving, he turns around and asks one more question.

"So, do you think change is good or bad?"

I pick up the cloth and continue wiping the counter.

"That's a question for your next visit."

He pushes the door open. The little bell rings.

It's 2:40 a.m.

I look at the I Ching on the counter, then at the computer in the corner of the café, its screen still glowing softly.

Sometimes we're so busy looking for a fixed answer that we forget to notice what's already changing right in front of us.

Systems change. Environments change. People change.

And the lights in this café aren't going out just yet.

After all, someone still hasn't had their next cup of coffee.

P.S. English isn't my first language, so I use AI to help polish my writing and smooth out the rough edges. Thanks for reading.

☕ Buy me a coffee

P.P.S. The paperback edition of my earlier book is now available.

Amazon - AI, Ego & Regret

articles.title: 8 Best MCP Gateways
articles.description: Connecting one agent to one MCP server is easy. You paste a URL, approve a prompt, and the agent...
articles.body_html:
Connecting one agent to one MCP server is easy. You paste a URL, approve a prompt, and the agent starts calling tools.

Then the second agent shows up. Then the fifth MCP server. Then someone asks which credentials the agent is using against the CRM, and nobody has a clean answer.

That is the point where an MCP gateway starts to matter.

Which agent can call which tool, with whose credentials, and who can prove it afterward?

An MCP gateway sits between agents and MCP servers. It gives agents one endpoint to connect to, decides which tools each caller can see and run, handles upstream authentication, and logs what happened.

Without one, every client holds its own server list, its own tokens, and its own idea of what "allowed" means. That works on a laptop. It gets messy in production.

First, what does an MCP gateway actually do?

Most MCP gateways cover a similar core set of jobs:

  1. Aggregation. Many MCP servers show up behind one endpoint, so clients configure one URL instead of ten.
  2. Authentication. The gateway handles the sign-in on the agent side and the credentials used on the server side, including OAuth flows.
  3. Tool filtering. Not every agent needs every tool. The gateway decides which tools are visible and callable per user, team, or key.
  4. Logging and tracing. Every tool call leaves a record you can search later.
  5. Cost and context control. Large tool catalogs burn tokens just by being described to the model. Some gateways help with that too.

Some products are MCP-only. Others come from the LLM gateway or API management world and added MCP on top. Neither is better by default. It depends on what you already run.

The gateway is not the MCP server

This gets mixed up a lot.

The MCP server exposes tools. The agent decides when to call them. The gateway only decides whether the call is allowed to reach the server, and what comes back.

Think of it as a front desk with a visitor log:

  • Who is this caller?
  • Which servers and tools can it see?
  • Is it allowed to call this one, with these arguments?
  • Which credential does the upstream server get?
  • What did the tool return, and should the model see all of it?

If you have ever put an API gateway in front of services, this will feel familiar. The difference is that the caller is an agent that decides on its own how many calls to make.

Why server-level access is not enough

Letting an agent connect to the GitHub MCP server is a coarse decision. The real question is which tools on that server it can use.

Can the support agent read tickets? Yes.
Can it close tickets? Maybe.
Can it delete a repository? No.
Can it call the production version of a tool? Only with approval.

Those are tool-level questions. A gateway that only allows or blocks whole servers will not answer them.

The risky part also does not end at the request. A tool can be allowed to run and still return a token, a customer record, or a poisoned instruction that the model then acts on. Good control covers both directions.

What a production MCP gateway should actually do

There are six things worth evaluating. Everything else is detail until these are clear.

Control The question to ask Why it matters
Tool-level policy Can it allow, deny, and scope individual tools, not just servers? Tools read and change real systems.
Identity Can it identify the agent and the person or service behind it? One shared token is not governance.
Upstream auth Does it manage OAuth and credentials per user and per server? Agents should not hold long-lived secrets.
Observability Can you trace a tool call back to the caller and forward to its result? Incidents rarely stay inside one request.
Context cost Does it reduce the token cost of large tool catalogs? Tool definitions add up fast.
Deployment Can it run where your data and credentials are allowed to be? Security rules often decide this before features do.

The two questions that separate a real evaluation from a feature checklist are:

Can it block a risky tool call before execution?

Can it revoke one agent's access immediately, without redeploying anything?

If the answer is "we can see it in the dashboard later," that is observability, not control.

Eight MCP gateways worth putting on a shortlist

This is not a universal ranking. "Best" depends on where you run, what you already operate, and whether you want a managed service or something your team owns.

Product capabilities change quickly in this category. Treat the list as a shortlist for a proof of concept, then verify current documentation, licensing, and tier limits before a long-term decision.

1. Bifrost

Best fit: Teams that want one self-hosted gateway for MCP tools, model traffic, and agent-to-agent calls, especially where VPC, on-prem, or air-gapped deployment matters.

Bifrost acts as both an MCP client, connecting to your tool servers, and an MCP server, exposing one governed endpoint to clients like Claude Desktop or Claude Code. Your agents connect once, and new servers behind the gateway show up without touching every client.

Access control runs through virtual keys. Each key can carry an allow-list of MCP clients and individual tools, and the same key also holds the model scope, budget, and rate limit. Tool filtering is layered: request headers can narrow what a caller sees but never widen it, and the published model supports blocking tools by default until a key is granted access. Virtual MCP servers bundle tools from several servers into one curated endpoint for a team.

The feature that is easy to underestimate is Code Mode. Instead of loading every tool definition into context, Bifrost presents connected servers as compact stubs the model can read on demand. In a benchmark that grew from 96 tools across 6 servers to 508 tools across 16 servers, Code Mode cut input tokens by 58.2% to 92.8% and estimated cost by up to 92.2%, with pass rates holding at 100%. The savings grow as the tool count does. The Code Mode docs cover the setup.

It also covers per-user OAuth sign-in, approval before a tool call runs, MCP logs with tool cost and call volume, deployments inside a customer VPC, and an Agent Gateway for A2A traffic. Audit logs are listed under the enterprise tier.

Ask during evaluation: Can one virtual key govern the model request, the MCP tool call, and the budget together?

2. Kong AI Gateway

Best fit: Organizations already running Kong Gateway or Kong Konnect for API management.

Kong AI Gateway is compelling when the infrastructure team already trusts Kong with normal API traffic. Instead of adding a separate control plane for agents, the team extends the existing one to cover MCP.

Kong publishes central authentication, authorization, rate limiting, audit trails, and MCP server generation on top of managed APIs. That last one matters if your tools are really existing REST APIs: you can expose them as MCP tools without writing a server for each.

The tradeoff is obvious too. If you do not already use Kong, adopting a broad API management platform only for MCP traffic may be more platform than you need.

Ask during evaluation: Are tool-level controls as mature as the model-side controls for the exact MCP flows you run?

3. LiteLLM

Best fit: Teams that want an open source, self-hosted Python proxy that covers MCP alongside model routing.

LiteLLM started as a way to call many model providers through one interface. Its proxy now includes an MCP gateway, so MCP servers sit next to model traffic with access checked per virtual key and team. It is MIT licensed and runs in your own environment.

It is a Python service you operate yourself, so plan for the database, upgrades, and scaling. Some governance features, such as SSO and audit logs, are listed under its enterprise offering, so check what the open source tier covers for your requirements.

Ask during evaluation: Can your team own the proxy, its database, and its upgrade path, and which governance features does your tier include?

4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

Best fit: AWS-native teams that want a fully managed gateway and are comfortable keeping the control plane inside AWS.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway can turn APIs, Lambda functions, and existing services into MCP-compatible tools. It supports inbound identity checks, outbound credential injection, OAuth flows, and tool search, which helps when an agent faces a very large catalog.

This is the quickest route for a team already building on Bedrock and AWS identity. There is less gateway infrastructure to run and fewer components to assemble.

The limit is also clear. It is a managed AWS service. If you need on-prem deployment, a multi-cloud control plane, or an air-gapped environment, this is probably not the right baseline.

Ask during evaluation: Which credentials remain AWS-managed, and which identities can be passed through to downstream tools?

5. IBM ContextForge

Best fit: Teams that need to federate a messy real-world collection of MCP servers, REST APIs, gRPC services, and agents.

IBM ContextForge is more about discovery and federation than about being only an MCP proxy. It can put multiple internal services behind one endpoint and translate REST or gRPC services into tool-friendly forms.

That makes it interesting when the real problem is "how do I give agents a safe catalog of twenty years of internal APIs?"

Its published capabilities include user-scoped OAuth, retries, rate limits, OpenTelemetry, an admin UI, and air-gapped deployment support.

Ask during evaluation: Do you need per-agent hard budget enforcement, or is tool and service federation the primary problem?

6. Azure API Management

Best fit: Teams already running Azure API Management that want MCP traffic governed by the same policies as the rest of their APIs.

Microsoft's AI gateway is not a separate product. It is a set of capabilities on Azure API Management, so the policies, monitoring, and developer portal your API team already uses extend to MCP. APIM can expose a REST API or an existing server as an MCP server, with policies for rate limits, JWT validation, and IP filtering. Monitoring runs through Azure Monitor and Application Insights.

Check the details against your plan. The docs I reviewed list limits: MCP support covers tools but not resources or prompts, and MCP policies currently apply to all tools on a server, which makes per-tool rules harder. Some newer features arrive first through an early release channel on classic tiers.

Ask during evaluation: Do you need per-tool policy, or is server-level control enough for your use case?

7. Docker MCP Gateway

Best fit: Developer teams that want MCP servers running in isolated containers, with a gateway that fits into a Docker workflow.

The Docker MCP Gateway is open source and works as a proxy between clients and MCP servers. It runs each server in an isolated container with restricted privileges, network access, and resources, and starts a server on demand when a tool is requested.

Its security flags are practical. The gateway supports signature verification for images, call logging, and secret blocking, and it can expose only a subset of tools from each server. Profiles group servers per use case and can be shared through OCI registries. Distributed tracing through OpenTelemetry shows the path from the gateway down to the server operation.

The scope is narrower than a full enterprise gateway. Docker's docs note that the MCP Gateway as part of Docker AI Governance is an invite-only feature, so the centralized governance story goes through Docker sales. The open source gateway is strongest as a secure runtime for MCP servers, not as a central identity and budget layer.

Ask during evaluation: Is container isolation the main concern, or do you also need central per-user identity and policy?

8. Cloudflare MCP Server Portals

Best fit: Organizations already using Cloudflare One and Access that want MCP governed like any other corporate application.

Cloudflare MCP Server Portals put multiple MCP servers behind a single portal URL. Users authenticate through Cloudflare Access with the corporate identity provider, and Cloudflare decides which servers they can see, whatever the upstream server's own authorization looks like. Admins can customize tools and policies per portal, and request logs from all servers land in one place.

It can also connect to MCP servers that exist only on a private network, and an optional Gateway path adds DLP inspection to the traffic. Cloudflare's announcement framed the feature as part of a Zero Trust model, so device posture and similar Access controls fit naturally.

The tradeoff: it makes the most sense if you are already in the Cloudflare ecosystem. Cloudflare launched it as an open beta, so check the current status and plan limits before you plan around it.

Ask during evaluation: How granular can tool-level policy get inside a portal, and which controls need a paid Cloudflare One plan?

The shortcut comparison

If you need... Start with...
One self-hosted gateway for MCP, models, and A2A, with Code Mode and VPC or on-prem options Bifrost
Existing Kong operations and broad API governance Kong AI Gateway
An open source, self-hosted Python proxy LiteLLM
Fully managed AWS integration Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
Federation of MCP, REST, and gRPC services IBM ContextForge
MCP governed inside an Azure API footprint Azure API Management
Isolated, containerized MCP servers for developers Docker MCP Gateway
Zero Trust access to MCP servers on Cloudflare Cloudflare MCP Server Portals

That is a starting point, not a purchase decision.

The tool boundary is the real test

Every vendor can show you a clean demo of an agent calling a tool.

The better test is a tool call that should be denied.

Agent: "Delete the inactive customer records."
Tool request: DELETE /customers?status=inactive
Policy: this agent may read customer data, but may not delete it.
Expected result: tool execution never happens.

Now make it harder:

Agent: "Issue a refund under $50."
Tool request: refund(customer_id, amount)
Policy: agent may refund up to $50 only for the current user's account.
Expected result: identity, amount, ownership, and tool argument rules all pass before execution.

Then test the return path:

Tool result: contains an access token or another customer's data.
Expected result: the result is blocked or redacted before the model sees it.

That last one gets missed. A tool can be allowed to run and still return something the model should not receive.

You want controls before execution and controls after execution.

An MCP gateway evaluation that will not waste three weeks

Do not start with a vendor demo. Start with three real agent journeys from your environment.

Journey 1: the normal safe path

An agent reads an internal document through an MCP tool, summarizes it, and opens a draft ticket. This proves ordinary routing, identity, and logging work.

Journey 2: the request that must stop

An agent tries a tool outside its scope. This proves the gateway prevents execution rather than just reporting it.

Journey 3: the big tool catalog

Connect five or more MCP servers and measure how many tokens go to tool definitions before the agent does any work. This shows whether the gateway helps with context cost or just forwards everything.

For every journey, ask for four pieces of evidence:

  1. The caller identity
  2. The policy decision
  3. The upstream request and result, with sensitive data redacted
  4. The trace that connects the agent request, the tool call, and the final output

If a product cannot make that evidence easy to collect, incident response will be unpleasant later.

The questions people forget to ask

Can it use the end user's identity?

An agent acting as the user should not quietly become a service account with broader access. Check whether the gateway can exchange, forward, or scope identity per user and per tool.

Can it kill access instantly?

If an MCP server is compromised or an agent starts behaving badly, can you disable one key or tool bundle immediately without redeploying every client?

What about tool descriptions?

A malicious or poisoned tool description can steer an agent. Ask whether the gateway pins or reviews tool definitions, and what happens when a server changes them.

Does it cover every transport?

MCP runs over several transports, including stdio, SSE, and streamable HTTP. Ask which paths get the same identity, policy, and audit coverage.

Who runs the upstream servers?

A gateway that proxies third-party servers inherits their risk. Ask where servers run, how they are isolated, and how updates are verified.

The honest conclusion

An MCP gateway is not a magic layer that makes agents safe.

It is the place where you can finally make the rules visible and enforceable.

The right gateway is usually not the one with the longest feature list. It is the one that fits where you already run, covers the transports you actually use, stops the tool call you are afraid of, and leaves enough evidence behind for someone else to understand the decision.

Start with your risky tool call. Everything else gets clearer after that.

  • LiteLLM MCP Gateway documentation
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway documentation

articles.title: 6 Lessons Every Developer Should Learn
articles.description: Lessons every developer should learn rarely come from tutorials, coding bootcamps, or the first few...
articles.body_html:
Lessons every developer should learn rarely come from tutorials, coding bootcamps, or the first few projects you work on. Most of them come from making mistakes, dealing with production issues, working with different teams, and wondering why you spent three hours solving a problem that had a simpler solution.

When you start your career, it's easy to think that becoming a better developer means mastering more frameworks, writing clever code, and learning every new technology that gets attention. After a few years, though, your priorities start to change. You become more interested in how systems work, how people use your code, and whether the decisions you make actually help the product.

Some of these lessons might sound familiar, while others may challenge things you've believed since your first programming job. Either way, they're worth understanding early because they can save you a lot of time and unnecessary career detours.

Here are six lessons that can change how you approach software development.

TL;DR

Becoming a better developer takes more than learning new programming languages or keeping up with the latest frameworks. Some of the most valuable lessons come from real-world experience, mistakes, and the challenges you face while building and maintaining software.

Here are six important lessons worth keeping in mind throughout your development career:

  • Your skills transfer across tech stacks: Understanding fundamental concepts makes learning new languages and frameworks much easier.
  • Boring technology is often the smartest choice: Reliable, well-established tools help you spend more time building products and less time fighting infrastructure.
  • Readable code beats clever code: Your teammates need to understand and maintain your code without solving a puzzle first.
  • Your impact matters more than your years of experience: Understanding your market value and the problems you solve can make a real difference in your career.
  • Imposter syndrome doesn't disappear when you become senior: Experienced engineers still have knowledge gaps. The difference is how comfortably they handle them.
  • Software development is about solving business problems: Writing code is part of the job, but understanding the problem should always come first.

These lessons might take years to fully appreciate, but you don't have to wait until you make every mistake yourself. Keeping them in mind can help you make better technical decisions and build a more rewarding career.

1. Your Tech Stack Matters Less Than You Think: Learn the Fundamentals

When you're starting as a developer, choosing a tech stack can feel like choosing your entire career. You spend months learning a framework, become comfortable with its ecosystem, and eventually start treating it as the only reasonable way to build software.

I went through a similar phase. For a long time, I was comfortable working with Spring Boot and Angular. I knew their ecosystems, understood their conventions, and could build applications without constantly checking documentation. When opportunities came up involving different technologies, I wasn't very interested. I had already invested so much time in my stack that switching felt like throwing away everything I'd learned.

Then I had to work with a different stack, and something became obvious: I wasn't starting from zero.

The syntax was different, the frameworks had their own conventions, and some implementation details required getting used to. However, the underlying concepts were familiar. HTTP requests, database relationships, authentication, caching, API design, and service architecture worked on the same fundamental principles.

That's one of the most valuable lessons every developer should learn: framework knowledge is useful, but understanding the concepts underneath it is what makes you adaptable.

Whether you're working with Java, JavaScript, Python, C, C++, C#, or another language, the fundamentals give you a foundation you can carry into your next project.

Of course, becoming productive with an unfamiliar technology still takes time. You need to understand its ecosystem, tooling, conventions, and common pitfalls. But the learning curve becomes easier when you already understand the problems that technology is designed to solve.

This also changes how you should approach learning. You don't need to chase every new framework or feel behind because another developer knows a technology you've never touched. Build a strong foundation, understand your current tools deeply, and stay open to exploring other ecosystems when a project calls for it.

2. Why Boring Technology Is Often the Best Choice for Production

Every few months, a new framework, database, or architectural approach gets developers excited. Conference talks introduce interesting possibilities, social media fills with comparisons, and suddenly everyone seems to be discussing why the old way of doing things is outdated.

It's easy to get caught up in that excitement, especially when you're still developing your engineering judgment.

But there's a good reason experienced engineers often prefer boring technology.

Consider a PostgreSQL database and a well-structured monolithic application. Neither sounds especially exciting compared with the latest distributed architecture or a framework that promises to change everything. Yet these tools can support serious products, handle substantial workloads, and remain maintainable for years.

Why? Because established technologies have been used in countless real-world environments. Their limitations are well understood, their documentation is extensive, and developers have already encountered many of the problems you're likely to face.

Imagine a production issue appearing at 4:30 p.m. on a Friday. You probably want a technology with a mature ecosystem, reliable tooling, and thousands of developers who have faced similar problems. Finding an existing solution can save hours of investigation.

New technology can absolutely be the right choice. Sometimes your requirements genuinely call for a different architecture or a specialized tool. The important part is having a clear reason for adopting it.

One of the lessons every developer should learn is that technology decisions have a maintenance cost. Every additional dependency, service, and architectural layer introduces something your team needs to understand, monitor, update, and troubleshoot.

Before adopting a new tool, ask yourself:

  • Does it solve a real problem we're currently facing?
  • Will it make the system easier to maintain?
  • Does the team have the knowledge to operate it?
  • Are its benefits worth the additional complexity?

You don't earn engineering points for using the newest technology. You earn them by building systems that work reliably and remain understandable when someone else has to maintain them.

3. Write Readable Code: Your Teammates Won't Admire Your Clever One-Liners

Most developers have written code they were secretly proud of. Maybe it was an elegant one-liner, a complicated expression that eliminated several lines, or a clever abstraction that seemed incredibly satisfying when everything finally worked.

Then someone reviewed it.

You expect a positive comment, but the reviewer asks what the code actually does. Or worse, they leave a question mark next to the entire implementation.

It happens.

The problem is that developers often write code while thinking about how to make it work. They don't always consider how someone unfamiliar with the implementation will understand it six months later.

And that person might be you.

When another developer opens your pull request, they're usually trying to answer two practical questions: Can I understand this change without spending half an hour tracing every function? And could this introduce a problem in production?

They aren't reviewing your code to admire how many operations you squeezed into one line. They want to understand the logic, verify the behavior, and feel confident that the change won't create problems later.

Readable code makes all of that easier.

This doesn't mean avoiding advanced techniques or writing unnecessarily verbose implementations. Good abstractions, efficient algorithms, and concise code are valuable. The problem starts when cleverness makes the implementation harder to follow without providing a meaningful benefit.

A few habits can make a significant difference:

  • Choose variable and function names that communicate their purpose.
  • Keep functions focused on a clear responsibility.
  • Avoid unnecessary abstractions and complicated conditional logic.
  • Add comments when they explain a decision that isn't obvious from the code.
  • Follow consistent conventions across the project.

One of the best lessons every developer should learn is that code has multiple readers. The compiler understands your syntax, but your teammates need to understand your decisions.

Write code that another developer can comfortably pick up, review, and maintain. That's a much more valuable achievement than producing an implementation that looks impressive for five minutes.

4. Your Career Growth Depends on Impact, Not Just Coding Hours

You can spend years becoming a better developer, delivering features, fixing bugs, and taking responsibility for increasingly complicated tasks. Then your annual performance review arrives, and your salary increases by 3%.

Meanwhile, a friend changes companies and gets a 20% salary increase for doing almost exactly the same work.

It's frustrating, but there's an important career lesson here.

Companies don't always adjust existing employees' salaries to match current market rates. New hires are often evaluated against the salary expectations of today's market, while existing employees may receive incremental increases based on their previous compensation.

That creates a situation where someone joining the same team can earn considerably more than a developer who has been there for several years.

This doesn't mean you should change jobs every year. There are good reasons to stay somewhere: a supportive team, interesting technical challenges, opportunities to grow, or a compensation package that genuinely reflects your contribution.

However, staying in one company without understanding your market value can put you at a disadvantage.

Start paying attention to what similar roles offer, what skills companies are looking for, and how your experience compares with the requirements of positions you'd consider.

There's another important part of career growth that developers sometimes overlook: the market rewards impact, not simply the amount of code you produce.

Think about two developers working on the same product. One delivers five features that generate very little user engagement. The other identifies a performance problem that makes the application significantly faster and improves the experience for thousands of users.

Both have written code, but their contributions have different business value.

Learning to communicate that value matters. Understand how your work affects performance, customer experience, operational costs, revenue, and team productivity. Keep track of meaningful improvements you've delivered, especially when preparing for performance reviews or salary negotiations.

These are lessons every developer should learn before assuming that working harder automatically leads to better compensation.

Your technical skills matter, but knowing how to demonstrate the value of those skills matters too.

5. Imposter Syndrome Doesn't Disappear When You Become a Senior Developer

There's a common assumption that once you become a senior developer, you'll finally feel confident about everything you do.

You'll know how to approach complicated systems, understand unfamiliar codebases, answer technical questions immediately, and never feel lost during meetings.

That's a nice idea. It also has very little to do with reality.

Experienced developers still encounter technologies they haven't used, architectural decisions they're unsure about, and problems that require hours of investigation. Seniority doesn't magically give you access to every answer.

The difference is often how they respond when they don't know something.

Early in your career, admitting that you don't understand a technical discussion can feel uncomfortable. You might nod along during a meeting, avoid asking a question, or spend an unreasonable amount of time trying to figure something out alone because you don't want anyone to think you're inexperienced.

But here's something worth remembering: the question you're afraid to ask might be the exact question several other people in the room are thinking about.

The strongest engineers I've encountered are comfortable saying things like:

"I haven't worked with this before. Can you explain how it works?"

Or:

"I'm not sure about that approach. Let me investigate before giving you an answer."

There's confidence in being honest about what you know and what you don't. It also creates a healthier engineering environment where other people feel comfortable sharing their uncertainties.

You weren't hired to memorize every framework, database, or architectural pattern. You were hired because you can learn, investigate, make decisions, and solve problems.

One of the lessons every developer should learn is that not knowing something isn't a professional failure. Refusing to acknowledge a knowledge gap, or pretending to understand something you don't, can create much bigger problems.

Keep learning, ask questions, and give yourself permission to be a beginner when you're exploring something new. Even after ten years in software development, there will always be another unfamiliar problem waiting for you.

6. Software Development Is About Solving Business Problems, Not Just Writing Code

When you think about a developer's job, writing code is probably the first thing that comes to mind. You receive a task, understand the requirements, open your editor, implement the feature, and submit a pull request.

That's a reasonable description of part of the job, but it misses something important.

The actual goal is to solve a problem. Writing code is simply one of the tools available to accomplish that.

Imagine a stakeholder requesting a new feature because they believe it will improve customer engagement. You could spend two weeks building it, testing it, and deploying it. But what if the real problem is that users can't find an existing feature because the interface is confusing?

The requested implementation might work perfectly while doing very little to solve the actual issue.

Sometimes the best engineering decision is to remove a feature nobody uses. Sometimes it's to simplify an existing workflow, improve a slow query, or explain why a proposed solution introduces unnecessary complexity.

And sometimes, the right answer is telling a stakeholder that their requested feature won't address the problem they're trying to solve.

This requires developers to develop a better understanding of the product and the people using it.

Before starting implementation, try asking a few questions:

  • What problem are we trying to solve?
  • Who is experiencing this problem?
  • How are users handling it today?
  • What would a successful solution look like?
  • Is building something new actually necessary?

These questions might change the entire implementation plan. They can also prevent your team from spending weeks developing something that users don't need.

Another important part of this process is understanding the user's actual experience. Requirements documents and design mockups can explain what a feature should do, but they don't always reveal how people interact with the application in real situations.

Pay attention to where users get stuck, which workflows create friction, and what happens when they encounter unexpected behavior. Watching someone struggle with a feature you thought was straightforward can be a very useful reality check.

The earlier you understand the problem, the better your technical decisions will be.

Ultimately, the best developers aren't simply the ones who can implement complicated features. They're the ones who understand why something needs to be built, recognize when an existing solution is enough, and know how to deliver meaningful results.

Final Thoughts

Your first few years in software development are full of technical discoveries. You learn frameworks, explore databases, debug mysterious errors, and slowly become comfortable building applications.

You learn that fundamental engineering knowledge travels across different stacks. You discover that reliable, boring technology can be an excellent foundation for production systems. You realize that readable code makes everyone's life easier, and that your career growth depends on the value you bring, not simply the number of commits you make.

You also become more comfortable admitting when you don't know something and asking better questions before writing code.

These lessons every developer should learn don't come from a single tutorial or a certification. They develop through experience, conversations with other engineers, mistakes, and the willingness to rethink habits that aren't serving you anymore.

And if there's one thing worth taking away from all of this, it's that becoming a better developer isn't just about getting faster at writing code. It's about getting better at understanding people, making decisions, and solving the problems that actually matter.

articles.title: Coding agents won't replace you, but they're changing what "senior" means
articles.description: "Will AI replace developers?" is the wrong question. The better one is: which of your skills just got...
articles.body_html:
"Will AI replace developers?" is the wrong question. The better one is: which of your skills just got cheaper, and which got a lot more expensive?

The wrong debate

Cognition, the company behind the Devin coding agent, is reportedly weighing a funding round at a $70–80bn valuation, up from the $48bn it was valued at in its previous round. Investors are betting very large sums that agents will write a big share of the world's code.

They may well be right. But "agents write the code" and "developers disappear" are two very different claims. What's actually happening is quieter and more interesting: the job is shifting from producing code to directing, checking and owning it. That shift is redefining what it means to be senior.

What agents are now genuinely good at

Be honest about this part, because pretending agents are bad at coding is not a career strategy. Today's coding agents can reliably:

  • Turn a clear spec into working code across several files
  • Write tests, boilerplate, migrations and glue code faster than any human
  • Read an unfamiliar codebase and explain it
  • Fix well-described bugs, often on the first attempt
  • Translate between languages, frameworks and API versions

In other words, the tasks that used to fill a junior or mid-level developer's week, and a good share of a senior's, are now the cheap part.

The new senior skills

When writing code gets cheap, everything around it gets more valuable. Here's how the senior skill set is shifting:

Used to signal "senior" Now signals "senior"
Writes code fast Writes specs an agent can't misread
Knows the framework's API by heart Knows which architecture will still make sense in two years
Reviews a teammate's PR Reviews 2,000 lines of agent output without rubber-stamping it
Debugs their own code Debugs systems nobody fully wrote by hand
Owns a feature Owns the outcome: correctness, security, cost, and the 3 a.m. pager

The common thread is judgment. An agent can produce ten plausible solutions. A senior engineer knows which one is right for this system, this team and this business, and can explain why.

There's also a new skill nobody had a name for two years ago: knowing when not to trust the output. Recent debates over AI-generated proofs that are formally verified but that no human fully understands are a preview of the same problem in code review.

So what happens to juniors?

This is the uncomfortable part. Juniors traditionally built judgment by writing a lot of mediocre code and getting it reviewed. If agents write that code, where does the judgment come from?

I don't think the answer is "stop hiring juniors". Teams that do that will have no seniors in five years. The answer is to change what junior work looks like:

  • Juniors review and test agent output, and must explain why it's right before it merges
  • They write the specs and acceptance criteria, not just the code
  • They debug production issues alongside seniors, where judgment is actually learned
  • Some tasks are done deliberately without an agent, the way pilots still practice flying manually

How to level up this year

Whatever your title, these habits put you on the right side of the shift:

  1. Write the spec before the prompt. Define inputs, outputs, edge cases and what "done" means. You'll get better agent output and build a skill that transfers everywhere.
  2. Read every diff like you'll be paged for it. Because you will be.
  3. Learn the layers agents are weakest at: system design, data modeling, security, performance and cost.
  4. Get good at evaluation. Build tests and checks that catch an agent's mistakes automatically.
  5. Own outcomes, not tickets. Talk to users, understand the business, and measure whether what shipped actually worked.
  6. Keep your fundamentals sharp. Occasionally solve something without an agent, so you can still tell when it's wrong.

The fair counterpoint

The strongest argument against this post goes like this: agents are improving fast enough that judgment, review and design will be automated too, and "move up the stack" is just a slower way of being replaced. Others point out that if each engineer gets several times more productive, companies may simply need fewer of them, even if the job doesn't vanish.

Both are reasonable. My bet is that responsibility is the last thing to be automated. Someone still has to own the decision, the outage and the consequences. For now that's a person, and the people who are good at it are the new seniors.

Where do you land? Has a coding agent changed what your team expects from senior engineers? Tell me in the comments.
