articles.title: Your agent's tool registry is an API. Stop reviewing it like config.
articles.description: Most agent security conversations start with the model. Can it be jailbroken? Will it follow an...
articles.body_html:
Most agent security conversations start with the model. Can it be jailbroken? Will it follow an instruction buried in a scraped web page? Those are real questions. They are also the wrong place to stop.

An agent's risk is shaped by what it can do, not only by what it decides. The model picks a tool. The tool carries the authority. If you only review the first half of that sentence, you are reviewing the part you control least.

The demo vs. production gap

In the demo, the agent has three tools: search_docs, get_weather, summarize. Nothing it calls can hurt anyone.

In production, the tool list grows one PR at a time. Someone adds create_ticket. Someone else adds run_sql "for internal analytics". A third person swaps the read-only GitHub token for one with full repo scope because the agent needs to open PRs now. None of these changes touched a route file, so none of them got the review a new public endpoint would get.

That's the gap. The tool registry is API surface. It just doesn't look like it.

Four questions for every tool

For each tool the agent can call, answer these:

  1. What kind of action is it? Read, write, execute, or trigger something external (email, payment, webhook, deploy). These are different risk classes and should be labeled that way.
  2. Whose identity does it run as? The end user's delegated identity? A shared service account? The agent's own credential with org-wide scope?
  3. What data can it reach? Not what it's meant to reach. What the credential and the query surface actually allow.
  4. Where is approval required? Is there a human-in-the-loop step, and is it enforced in the tool layer, or only suggested in the system prompt?

If the answer to #4 lives only in the prompt, you don't have an approval step. You have a polite request for one.

Failure mode 1: the read tool that reads everything

(Illustrative scenario, not a real incident.) A support agent gets a lookup_customer(query) tool. It's labeled read-only, and that's true. Under the hood it calls an internal admin endpoint that accepts arbitrary filters. "Read-only" holds. "Scoped to the customer in this ticket" does not. One injected instruction in a ticket body and the agent is paginating through every account in the system.

The model did nothing exotic. It used the tool exactly as designed. The design granted too much.

Failure mode 2: the side effect nobody listed

(Illustrative.) update_order_status looks like a single row write. It also fires a webhook that emails the customer and, when the status is "cancelled", kicks off a refund workflow. The tool description mentions neither. Reviewers approved a database write. They shipped a refund button.

Side effects belong in the tool's contract, the same way you'd document them on a public endpoint.

Failure mode 3: identity drift

(Illustrative.) The agent's credential started as a read-scoped token. Over six months it picked up write access on two repos, admin on a Slack workspace, and a cloud role someone attached while debugging an incident and never removed. No single change looked alarming. The sum is an over-privileged service account that takes instructions in natural language.

Make authority visible in the diff

One practical fix: have every tool definition declare its authority explicitly, so a change in authority shows up as a change in the diff.

@tool(
    name="refund_order",
    action="external",          # read | write | execute | external
    identity="user_delegated",  # not "service_admin"
    data_scope="order:{order_id}",
    requires_approval=True,
)
def refund_order(order_id: str, amount_cents: int) -> RefundResult:
    ...

The decorator is pseudo-code, not a specific library. The point is that flipping requires_approval from True to False, or identity from user_delegated to service_admin, should be impossible to miss in review, and should be enforced at runtime by the tool layer rather than trusted to the model.

Then review it like any other API change:

  • CODEOWNERS on the tool registry, so security sees permission changes.
  • A CI check that fails when a tool's action class, identity, or approval flag changes without an explicit label.
  • Tests that call each tool with out-of-scope arguments and assert the call is refused.

The reframe

"Can the model choose this tool?" is one question. The harder one is: "If it does, what authority does the tool grant?"

An agent is a natural-language client for whatever API you hand it. Review that API like one.

How does your team review tool additions today? Is anyone treating the tool registry as API surface, or does it still ride along in the same PRs as prompt tweaks?

articles.title: Three Agents, One Repo: The Coordination Problem Nobody Designed For
articles.description: One coding agent is a productivity tool. Two agents in the same repository is a sociology experiment....
articles.body_html:
Three Agents, One Repo: The Coordination Problem Nobody Designed For

One coding agent is a productivity tool. Two agents in the same repository is a sociology experiment. Three is a coordination problem that most teams solve for the first time in production, on a Friday.

The infrastructure conversation covers fleet orchestration and control planes. It skips the boring, decisive question: what happens when two agents touch the same file at the same time, and who resolves what they did to each other?

The Three Collisions

The mechanical collision is the friendly one. Two agents edit the same lines, git refuses to merge, and the failure is loud. Everyone notices. This is the good case, because the system said no.

The semantic collision is the dangerous one. Agent A changes the meaning of a function's return value. Agent B, working from the old contract, builds a feature that reads it. The merge is clean. The tests each wrote still pass in isolation. The system now believes two incompatible things, and nothing failed anywhere.

The duplicate collision is the expensive one. Two agents, given overlapping tickets, build the same feature twice with different names. Both PRs look competent. One of them is pure waste, and until someone notices, both are load.

None of these are exotic. They are the exact failure modes human teams have, at a speed that breaks the human mechanisms we built to catch them.

The Human Mechanism We Forgot to Port

Human teams coordinate through standups, hallway conversations, and ownership maps. "I'm touching the auth module, don't start there." It is informal, inefficient, and it works.

Agents attend no standup. They hold no grudges, share no memory, and read no hallway. The coordination layer has to become explicit, which means it has to become infrastructure:

A claim queue. Work is assigned or claimed, and a claim is visible. No two agents start the same ticket because the ticket said who started it. This is a work queue, not a scheduler, and it can be a spreadsheet before it is a platform.

An ownership map. Which files, modules, and decisions belong to which stream of work. Agents respect boundaries they are told about. They cannot respect boundaries nobody wrote down.

A merge gate between agents. Agent PRs that touch adjacent areas wait for the earlier one to land. Serializing the hot paths costs throughput and buys correctness, which is a trade humans already make every day.

A human integration owner. When agent PRs collide, a person who owns the integration decides. Not because humans are faster. Because someone has to be accountable for the seam, and accountability does not delegate to a process.

💡 Pro-tip: the semantic collision is the one to design against first. The mechanical one announces itself. The semantic one ships clean, passes its own tests, and gets discovered by a customer. A shared contract check between agents working in the same area is worth more than any lock.

Where This Breaks Down

Two or three agents on one repo is not a fleet, and the interesting failures will not always reproduce on demand. Solo developers with a single agent can skip all of this. The problem arrives the first time someone parallelizes "funnel all the open tickets to the agents" without anyone asking which tickets share a codepath.

There is also a real risk of over-engineering: most teams need a claim queue and a merge order, not a control plane, on day one.

But the direction of travel is obvious. The team now includes non-human contributors, and every org-design problem humans ever had, multiplied by speed and stripped of social instinct, is coming to a repository near you.

How many agents touch your repo before the first collision, and who resolved it? Was it loud, or was it clean?

References

  1. The fleet-level version of this problem, and why agent fleets need a control plane: Kubernetes for Agents
  2. The gatekeeper pattern for what agents may do when they get there: I Stopped Trusting AI Agents With Tools. So I Built a Gatekeeper.

articles.title: pdf.js + pdf-lib bugs you only hit on real user PDFs
articles.description: pdf.js and pdf-lib look easy together on clean test PDFs. Then real scans, bank statements, and...
articles.body_html:
pdf.js and pdf-lib look easy together on clean test PDFs. Then real scans, bank statements, and 300-page forms show up.

Most of these bugs came up while I was building client-side PDF tools on BrowsersKit (splitting, merging, signing, and compressing). None of them showed up in my own generated fixtures.

Signatures land sideways on rotated scans (/Rotate + CropBox)

pdf.js renders pages through page.getViewport({ scale }). That viewport already applies the page's /Rotate flag and shifts coordinates to start at the CropBox origin.

pdf-lib does neither. page.drawImage() writes straight into unrotated page user space. On a normal A4 PDF you never notice, because /Rotate is 0 and CropBox starts at (0, 0). On a scanned contract with /Rotate 90 or 270, the user drags a signature onto the bottom-right corner and the exported file puts it sideways near the wrong edge.

In the helper below, s is already converted from canvas top-down Y into bottom-left visible PDF points (0..W, 0..H). We map it back into unrotated user space, and +r cancels the page rotation because /Rotate is clockwise while pdf-lib's degrees(r) rotates counter-clockwise around (x, y):

export function visibleToUserSpace(s, crop, angle) {
  const r = (((Math.round(angle / 90) * 90) % 360) + 360) % 360;
  const W = r % 180 === 0 ? crop.width : crop.height;
  const H = r % 180 === 0 ? crop.height : crop.width;
  let u = s.x;
  let v = s.y;
  if (r === 90) [u, v] = [H - s.y, s.x];
  else if (r === 180) [u, v] = [W - s.x, H - s.y];
  else if (r === 270) [u, v] = [s.y, W - s.x];
  return { x: crop.x + u, y: crop.y + v, rotate: degrees(r) };
}

One extra quirk on top of that: if a PDF sets /UserUnit, pdf.js scales the viewport by it while pdf-lib draws in raw user units. I divide the viewport's width and height by page.userUnit upfront so both the stamp coordinates and its width/height land in pdf-lib's coordinate space.

copyPages() blows up split forms from 1 MB to 71 MB

In pdf-lib, out.copyPages(src, [pageIndex]) copies annotations and form widgets on the page, but leaves /AcroForm empty in the output document. After merging or splitting a fillable form, the fields still look visible, except you can't type into them anymore.

Worse: copying a widget follows its /Parent field object, which pulls /Kids widgets from other pages, which point via /P to those other pages, whose /Parent page-tree nodes pull sibling pages across the rest of the document. On a 300-page form with a shared field across pages, my first split-to-single-pages test pulled almost the whole book into every single output file. It took 29 seconds and produced 71 MB of output (around 240 KB per one-page file).

I fixed it by cloning only the field tree for the pages being copied before calling copyPages, trimming /Kids to the widgets on those pages, breaking any /Parent cycles, and then attaching the cloned roots into /AcroForm /Fields in the destination doc along with /AcroForm defaults like /DR and /DA. The same 300-page split dropped from 29 seconds / 71 MB down to 0.3 seconds / 1.2 MB, and the fields stayed fillable. If you merge two copies of the same form, you also have to suffix colliding field names (_2, _3) so editing form B doesn't overwrite form A.

ignoreEncryption: true silently corrupts edit-locked bank PDFs

A lot of bank statements open fine in pdf.js with no password prompt, because they only carry a permissions lock (blocking edits, not viewing).

Hand that same file to PDFDocument.load(bytes) and pdf-lib throws an encrypted-document error. It's tempting to pass { ignoreEncryption: true } so the load succeeds. Don't do it. The streams and strings stay encrypted inside an output whose encryption metadata and object keys no longer match, and saving produces blank or garbled pages.

If you're sticking to plain pdf-lib without shipping a separate WASM decryptor, check await doc.getPermissions() on the already-opened pdf.js document right when the user drops the file (null means unencrypted, non-null means permission-locked) and fail immediately. Letting someone place signatures for two minutes only to blow up on Save is miserable.

Re-encoding embedded JPEGs breaks signatures, EXIF rotation, and wide-gamut colors

When I built the PDF compression tool by re-encoding embedded JPEGs through <canvas>, three things broke right away.

First, rewriting any PDF with /SigFlags (bit 1 set), /Perms, or /ByteRange invalidates its cryptographic signature, so viewers flag the file as modified. I detect signed PDFs upfront and skip recompression completely.

Second, browsers apply EXIF orientation when decoding a JPEG onto a canvas, while PDF viewers ignore EXIF inside embedded streams. Re-encoding an EXIF-oriented JPEG blindly saves it rotated or flipped wrong, so I parse the JPEG EXIF orientation header first and skip any stream with orientation > 1.

Third, PDF ignores ICC profiles stored inside embedded JPEG bytes and renders using the PDF Image XObject's own /ColorSpace entry (like /ICCBased Display P3). Decoding with default createImageBitmap() converts those pixels to sRGB, so writing them back under the preserved PDF /ColorSpace shifts colors. Passing { colorSpaceConversion: 'none' } keeps raw channel values aligned with the preserved /ColorSpace.

Forgetting page.cleanup() leaks gigabytes on thumbnails

If you render a thumbnail grid with pdf.js, call page.cleanup() in a finally block right after drawing each page. Without it, pdf.js keeps decoded bitmaps and fonts alive for every rendered page. On a 120-page 300 dpi scan, adding that single line cut peak RAM from 2.2 GB to 0.8 GB.

Architectural sheets make canvas.toBlob() return null

A 5m x 5m CAD sheet (14400 x 14400 pt) rendered at 2x asks the browser for a 28800 x 28800 canvas. It doesn't always throw right away; often toBlob() just passes null to its callback and crashes downstream.

I clamp the render scale against both a max side (16384 px) and a max pixel area (64 MP), and if toBlob() still fails on mobile Safari (which caps canvas area around 16.7 MP), I release the canvas (width = 0; height = 0) and retry once at 16 MP. Normal A4 to A2 pages at 2x stay well under the cap, and huge drawings stop killing the tab.

If you're shipping browser PDF tools, start hoarding ugly real-world PDFs on day one. Library-generated fixtures lie.

articles.title: The Stopped Flag Stops Nothing That Already Started
articles.description: After the reject, the workers keep looping. That is the hole in yesterday's pre-fill piece, and...
articles.body_html:
After the reject, the workers keep looping. That is the hole in yesterday's pre-fill piece, and sunnatulla_dev found it before I did. In his run, tasks 6 to 9 started at 301 to 421 milliseconds, after the call had already rejected at 272, and a second later every slot read ok. So the array calls them skipped, they ran, and anyone who retries them runs them twice. His fix is one line: set stopped = true in the catch, and let the workers check while (!stopped && ...) before picking up the next task.

I ran his version on the same shape. Ten tasks, three workers, task 4 throwing after 150 milliseconds. Same delays as yesterday, both arms twice, and both repeats came back identical. The flag works. It also leaves two tasks double-running, and those two are the interesting part.

Here is the shape, with the flag in:

async function mapWithConcurrency(tasks, limit) {
  const results = tasks.map(() => ({ status: "skipped" }));
  let next = 0, stopped = false;
  async function worker() {
    while (!stopped && next < tasks.length) {
      const i = next++;
      try {
        results[i] = await tasks[i]();
      } catch (err) {
        results[i] = { status: "failed", error: err.message };
        stopped = true;
        throw err;
      }
    }
  }
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: limit }, () => worker()));
  return results;
}

The reject lands at the same moment in both arms, 275 to 277 milliseconds across the four runs. The flag costs nothing on wall time, because it does not stop anything that is already running. It only stops new pickups, and there is nothing to pick up until a worker finishes a task.

No flag Stopped flag
Reject wall time 277 ms 277 ms
Tasks started after the reject 5 (tasks 5–9, at 302–743 ms) 0
Slots reading "skipped" at the reject 7 7
Slots reading "skipped" 1.2 s later 0 5
Tasks double-run by retrying the "skipped" slots 7 2

Read the no-flag row first, because it is worse than it sounds. At the reject, seven slots read skipped. A second later, none of them do. Tasks 5 to 9 started after the call had already failed and finished fine, and tasks 2 and 3 were still running when the reject landed and finished fine too. The array drifts under the caller. A retry built from the reject-time snapshot runs all seven again. Seven tasks doing real work twice, because the label was written before the work happened and nobody updated it after.

The flag arm fixes five of the seven. Tasks 5 to 9 never start. A second later they still read skipped, and this time the label is true: nothing ran there, nothing will, and a retry runs each of them exactly once. That is the whole win, and it is a real one. Five phantom runs gone, for one line and zero measurable cost.

But look at the last row. Two double-runs survive the flag, and they are tasks 2 and 3, the pair that was mid-flight when task 4 threw. The flag cannot reach them. They are inside an await when stopped flips to true, and the loop condition is only checked after the await resolves. They finish, they write ok into their slots, and the caller that read "skipped" at reject time retries them anyway. In my run they finished 24 and 44 milliseconds after the reject. The window is small. The double-run is not.

This is the part the one-line fix cannot close. The flag answers the question "has a worker picked this up yet" at the moment of the reject, and for the two in-flight tasks the honest answer at that moment is "yes, and it is not done". The array says skipped because nothing has written anything else yet. There are only two ways to tell the truth about those two slots. One is to mark a task "running" when the worker picks it up, so the caller can see the difference between untouched and in-flight and decide what a retry means for each. The other is to wait before retrying: let the stragglers land, read the array again, and retry only what still reads skipped after everything has settled. The first costs a line. The second costs a delay, and the delay is the honest price of a retry you can trust.

So sunnatulla_dev is right, and the flag is worth adding, and it is not the whole fix. Add it. It turns seven double-runs into two, for free. Then mark the in-flight tasks, or wait for them, because the two that survive are the ones doing real work when the batch falls over, and they are the ones a blind retry will run twice. A stopped flag stops the queue. It stops nothing that already started.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: How I Built an Undertale-Inspired Bad Time Simulator in Pure JavaScript (60 FPS on Browser)
articles.description: Every indie developer has that one passion project inspired by a game they love. For me, that...
articles.body_html:
Every indie developer has that one passion project inspired by a game they love. For me, that obsession was the notorious Sans genocide boss fight from Undertale.

If you've ever played it, you know the feeling: hours of muscle memory wiped out in seconds by a barrage of frame-perfect bones, spinning platforms, and laser-firing Gaster Blasters. The problem? If you want to practice specific attack patterns, you traditionally have to replay the entire game or mess around with local desktop save files.

I asked myself: Could I rebuild a pixel-perfect, deterministic bullet-hell engine right inside the web browser that runs at a locked 60 FPS without any downloads?

That idea led to the creation of Bad Time Simulator.

Here is the technical retrospective of how I engineered the engine, handled sub-pixel collision physics, optimized high-volume particle pooling, and brought retro bullet-hell mechanics to the modern web.

The Core Goals

Before writing a single line of code, I set three non-negotiable architectural requirements:

  1. Zero Input Latency: When dodging bullet hell, even a 16ms frame drop feels catastrophic.
  2. Sub-Pixel Deterministic Hitboxes: Replicating the distinct Red Soul (free directional flight) vs. Blue Soul (gravity-affected platformer physics) precision.
  3. Instant Accessibility: Lightweight, fully responsive across both desktop (keyboard) and mobile touchscreens.

The Tech Stack

I deliberately chose a lightweight, dependency-free architecture:

  • Rendering Layer: HTML5 Canvas 2D Context with offscreen double buffering (bypassing heavy third-party engine overhead).
  • Core Engine: Vanilla TypeScript/JavaScript using an explicit fixed-step requestAnimationFrame game loop.
  • Audio Engine: Web Audio API for zero-delay retro SFX playback and chiptune sound wave synchronization.
  • State & Attack Sequencing: Finite State Machine (FSM) defining procedural attack phases and bullet timing scripts.

Engineering Challenges & Solutions

1. Object Pooling for 200+ Active Projectiles

In the most frantic phases of the battle, the screen is flooded with moving bones, lasers, and particle debris. Allocating and destroying JavaScript objects inside the render loop causes frequent Garbage Collection (GC) pauses, resulting in micro-stutters.

To eliminate GC hitches, I implemented an Entity Object Pool:

class BonePool {
  constructor(initialSize = 300) {
    this.pool = Array.from({ length: initialSize }, () => new Bone());
    this.activeBones = [];
  }

  spawn(x, y, height, speedX, type = 'white') {
    const bone = this.pool.pop() || new Bone();
    bone.init(x, y, height, speedX, type);
    this.activeBones.push(bone);
    return bone;
  }

  recycle(bone) {
    const index = this.activeBones.indexOf(bone);
    if (index !== -1) {
      this.activeBones.splice(index, 1);
      bone.reset();
      this.pool.push(bone);
    }
  }
}

By reusing instantiated nodes, runtime heap allocation dropped to near-zero during combat loops, maintaining a solid 60 FPS on low-power mobile browsers.

2. The Dual-Soul Physics Engine

Recreating the two distinct movement states of the player soul required different physics models:

  • Red Soul (Omnidirectional Mode): Fixed velocity vector with instantaneous acceleration and deceleration.
  • Blue Soul (Gravity Mode): Standard jump-curve trajectory with gravity constants ($g$), terminal velocity caps, and AABB platform collision snapping. 
updateSoulPhysics(deltaTime) {
  if (this.mode === 'RED') {
    this.x += this.inputVector.x * this.speed * deltaTime;
    this.y += this.inputVector.y * this.speed * deltaTime;
  } else if (this.mode === 'BLUE') {
    // Apply gravity
    this.velocityY = Math.min(this.velocityY + this.gravity * deltaTime, this.terminalVelocity);
    this.y += this.velocityY * deltaTime;
    this.x += this.inputVector.x * this.horizontalSpeed * deltaTime;

    // Platform snapping check
    this.resolvePlatformCollisions();
  }
  this.clampToBounds(this.battleBox);
}

3. Audio & Beam Synchronization (The Gaster Blaster)

One of the most satisfying visual cues is the Gaster Blaster: it spawns, rotates toward the player, charges for a fixed duration, and beams down a wide column of damage.

To sync the visual beam expansion with the Web Audio sound explosion:

  • Audio samples are pre-decoded into memory buffers via AudioContext.decodeAudioData.
  • Sound trigger timestamps are locked to the FSM attack timeline rather than asynchronous DOM callbacks, guaranteeing audio-visual alignment down to the millisecond.

Live Demo & Try It Out

You can play, test your dodging skills, and practice attack patterns directly in your browser without any installation:

Try the Bad Time Simulator Here

Whether you want to warm up your reflexes or analyze how classic 2D retro bosses were constructed, give it a spin!

Lessons Learned & What's Next

Building this project reinforced a few key web game development truths:

  1. Canvas 2D is still remarkably fast: You don't always need complex WebGL shaders for retro 2D games; clean object lifecycle management and efficient math often provide better performance dividends.
  2. Deterministic timing is everything: Avoid tying game physics directly to fluctuating refresh rates (like 120Hz vs 60Hz displays). Always use a fixed-delta timestep loop.

Future roadmap:

  • [ ] Attack Pattern Editor: allowing players to design custom bullet-hell choreography via JSON.
  • [ ] Global Leaderboards for endless survival mode.
  • [ ] Gamepad / Controller API integration.

Have you ever rebuilt a retro game mechanic on the modern web? Let me know your thoughts or feedback in the comments below!

articles.title: Three date bugs in a 10-line age calculator (and the TZ= trick that exposes them)
articles.description: Age calculators look like a beginner exercise. Subtract the years, subtract the months, subtract the...
articles.body_html:
Age calculators look like a beginner exercise. Subtract the years, subtract the months, subtract the days, borrow when something goes negative. Mine had all of that. It still told a user born on 31 January that on 1 March they were 26 years, 1 month and −2 days old. On their birthday it said their next birthday was 365 days away.

Here are the three bugs and how I fixed them. If you've ever written new Date(input.value), at least one of them is probably in your code too.

Bug 1: new Date("2026-05-15") is not 15 May in your time zone

An <input type="date"> gives you a string like "2026-05-15". Passing that to new Date() creates midnight UTC, not local midnight. That's ECMAScript's rule for date-only ISO strings.

Then the code calls getDate(), getMonth() and so on, which read local time. In Pakistan (UTC+5) that UTC midnight is 05:00 on the same day, so the date looks right. But:

const nb = new Date(b.getFullYear(), a.getMonth(), a.getDate()); // local midnight
if (nb < b) nb.setFullYear(b.getFullYear() + 1);

On the birthday, nb is 00:00 local and b is 05:00 local, so nb < b is true and the next birthday jumps a year ahead. Hence "365 days".

In US time zones it's worse. UTC midnight is still the previous day locally, so every result was off by a day. The same inputs gave "1 month −2 days" in Lahore and "0 months 29 days" in Los Angeles.

Fix: parse the string yourself as a local calendar date.

function pd(v) {
  const [y, m, d] = v.split('-').map(Number);
  return new Date(y, m - 1, d);       // local midnight
}

The same trap applies the other way. input.valueAsDate = new Date() sets the field to today in UTC, which shows yesterday's date for anyone ahead of UTC just after midnight. Build the YYYY-MM-DD string from the local getFullYear/getMonth/getDate instead.

Bug 2: borrowing days from the wrong month

The classic algorithm:

let d = b.getDate() - a.getDate();
if (d < 0) {
  mo--;
  d += new Date(b.getFullYear(), b.getMonth(), 0).getDate(); // days in previous month
}

Born 31 Jan, today is 1 March: d = 1 - 31 = -30. Borrow February's 28 days and you get −2. The borrow assumes the previous month is long enough to absorb the difference, and February isn't.

Bug 3: there's no single "right" way to borrow, so define one

What is 31 January + 1 month? There's no 31 February. You have to choose, and the common choice (it's what most date libraries do) is to clamp to the last day of the month: 31 Jan + 1 month = 28 Feb, or 29 in a leap year.

Once you've chosen, the cleanest algorithm doesn't borrow at all. Count whole months, then count the leftover days:

function addMonths(t, n) {
  const y = t.getFullYear(), m = t.getMonth() + n;
  const last = new Date(y, m + 1, 0).getDate();          // last day of target month
  return new Date(y, m, Math.min(t.getDate(), last));     // clamp
}
function dayDiff(x, y) {                                   // DST-safe
  return Math.round((Date.UTC(y.getFullYear(), y.getMonth(), y.getDate())
                   - Date.UTC(x.getFullYear(), x.getMonth(), x.getDate())) / 864e5);
}
function age(a, b) {
  let months = (b.getFullYear() - a.getFullYear()) * 12 + (b.getMonth() - a.getMonth());
  if (addMonths(a, months) > b) months--;                  // this month's anniversary not reached
  const days = dayDiff(addMonths(a, months), b);
  return { years: Math.floor(months / 12), months: months % 12, days };
}

Days can never be negative now, because they're measured forward from the last whole-month anniversary. 31 Jan → 1 Mar is 1 month (to 28 Feb) plus 1 day.

The next birthday falls out of the same helper: addMonths(dob, 12 * yearsSince). That also handles 29 February birthdays (celebrated on the 28th in non-leap years).

How I tested it

  • Edge cases: month ends, 29 Feb in leap and non-leap years, the birthday itself, 31 Dec → 1 Jan.
  • Three time zones: each case ran under TZ=Asia/Karachi, TZ=America/Los_Angeles and TZ=UTC in Node. All three now print identical results. The old code gave a different answer in each zone I tried.
  • 20,000 random date pairs: asserting that days are never negative and months stay within 0–11.

The TZ= trick is the takeaway. If your date code gives different answers when you change the time zone of the machine running it, you have a bug, even if it looks fine where you live.

The calculator is part of 14FreeTools, a set of free tools that run entirely in the browser. People mostly use it to check job and admission age limits "as on" a closing date, where being one day off actually matters.

articles.title: I backtested "important questions" on 23 real exam papers. Topic prediction barely beat random.
articles.description: Every exam season, students at my university (AKTU, a state technical university in India with lakhs...
articles.body_html:
Every exam season, students at my university (AKTU, a state technical university in India with lakhs of engineering students) share "important questions" lists. Telegram channels, YouTube, coaching PDFs. Everyone claims their list covers "80% of the paper".

I run Ryzenstudy, a free archive of about 1,600 AKTU previous year papers. Since I already had the papers as OCR text, I wanted to know: does any of this actually work? So I built the obvious predictor and tested it the honest way, on papers it had never seen.

The setup

  • Data: OCR'd question text from AKTU end-semester papers, sessions 2021-22 to 2025-26.
  • Unit of analysis: every question row with its marks (Section A short, Section B medium, Section C long).
  • Labels: each question tagged with a syllabus topic and a "question family" (same question, reworded).
  • Predictor: rank topics by how often they appeared in earlier papers, call the top ones Tier 1 and Tier 2. This is basically what every "important questions" list does.
  • Test: blind backtest. For each of 10 B.Tech subjects, hide one paper, build tiers from the older papers only, then measure how many of the hidden paper's marks fall inside the predicted tiers. 23 held-out papers in total.
  • Baseline: a random set of topics of the same size. If the predictor can't beat that clearly, it isn't predicting anything.

The results

What I measured Result
Marks covered by Tier 1 + Tier 2 topics 61%
Marks covered by a random topic set of the same size 51%
Gain from weighting recent papers more < 1 point
Hidden-paper questions that matched an earlier question family 26%
Marks in a new paper that repeat an earlier question ~43%

Topic prediction gets you +10 points over random. That's it. A syllabus is small enough that any reasonable set of topics covers half the paper by accident, so "covers 60% of the paper" sounds impressive and means very little.

Recency weighting, the thing every "this year's expected questions" video leans on, did nothing measurable.

What actually holds up: repeats

The one number that survived is boring and useful: about 43% of a new paper's marks are questions that already appeared in an earlier paper (reworded, but the same question). For some subjects it's much higher. Electromagnetic Field Theory was 54%, Constitution of India 59%.

That's not prediction, it's just a fact about how papers get set. So I stopped calling anything "important" and built a repeat bank instead: every question that has appeared more than once, grouped by family, with the years it appeared.

You can see them here: AKTU important questions (repeat bank). Each subject page shows its own honest numbers, including the weak ones. Web Technology repeats only about 10%, and the page says so.

Things that broke along the way

  • OCR merges rows. Section A sub-questions (h), (i), (j) often came out as one line. I had to split them, or the marks totals went wrong.
  • Universities reuse subject codes. At AKTU, KCS502 was Compiler Design but BCS502 is Web Technology. Matching papers by code alone silently mixed two subjects, so I now match on code and title.
  • Partial papers poison the stats. A scan missing Section C makes a subject look like it has no long questions. Papers with fewer than 15 question rows are now excluded.
  • Maths is hard to OCR. For Engineering Mathematics, over 40% of the top questions came out as garbage, so those pages are held back instead of published with bad data.

Takeaways

  1. If someone sells "80% guaranteed" important questions, ask what their random baseline is.
  2. Solve previous year papers first, not prediction lists. Repeats are the only effect big enough to matter. All the papers I used are free here: AKTU previous year question papers.
  3. Backtest anything that claims to predict. It took me one evening to write the test, and it changed what I built.

If you've done something similar for your university's papers, I'd like to compare numbers.

articles.title: My pulse peaked when the practice tower cleared me to land
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge  My pulse climbed most when a...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

My pulse climbed most when a practice tower cleared me to land. The take-off clearance was not far behind.

I was at my desk with a headset on, talking to a simulated tower while the camera followed my pulse. Nothing was moving. Still, it was as if I could really see myself taking off, and then landing.

Both are short messages. The taxi clearance at the start is much longer: a runway, a QNH, a holding point and a route, to read back in order. In that session, my pulse didn't follow the length of the message. It followed what the words meant.

In October I built a practice tower for a friend who is shy about speaking English on the radio. It talks, it listens, and it says "negative" when the QNH is wrong. This month I pointed a camera at the person talking to it.

What I Built

Readback is a radio practice partner for student and private pilots. A simulated tower talks to you, and you read back out loud. Meanwhile, the camera follows your pulse and your breathing with the Presage SmartSpectra SDK.

Talking to the tower is one of the things that scare people when they learn to fly. You know the phraseology at home. Then a controller reads you a clearance in one breath, and you have to say it back, in order, while the frequency waits.

A session goes like this:

  1. A consent screen comes first. It says what is measured, what stays on the computer, what goes to Presage, and how to stop.
  2. A calm minute. You sit the way you will for the radio and breathe normally. That minute becomes your reference, for this session only.
  3. A circuit at Isola, a made-up aerodrome: taxi, take-off, a touch and go, a full stop. You hold the space bar to talk. The runway, the QNH and the wind change every game, and a wrong readback gets "negative".
  4. On the side, your pulse and your breathing, shown as differences from your calm minute.
  5. A breathing guide, if your breathing picked up while you listened. It offers three slow breaths before your readback. The tower waits.
  6. A timeline after the circuit. It puts first the messages after which your pulse climbed most.

It's a mirror for practice, not a measure of health. It compares you with yourself, and with nothing else. Like the October tower, it's a game, not an approved training device: your instructor and your country's phraseology manual are the reference.

Demo

The video shows the consent screen, the calm minute, an exchange with the tower, the breathing guide and the timeline. The camera preview is blurred.

Code

dsiacci / readback

Readback

A radio practice partner for student and private pilots. A simulated tower talks to you, you read back out loud, and the camera follows your pulse and your breathing while you do, with the Presage SmartSpectra SDK. Before your readback, if your breathing has picked up while you listened, a short breathing guide offers itself: the tower can wait. After the circuit, a timeline shows which messages made your pulse climb, next to what the tower said and what you read back.

A mirror for practice, not a measure of health. Readback compares you only with yourself, with a calm minute taken at the start of each session. It makes no medical claim, shows no normal or abnormal value, and never says whether anyone is fit to fly. It is a practice game, not an approved training device: your flight instructor and your country's official phraseology manual are…

View on GitHub

Electron and plain JavaScript, under the Apache 2.0 licence. On a Mac with Apple Silicon: npm install, then npm run setup:tower once, your Presage key in ~/.config/readback/presage.key, and npm start. No camera at hand? The first screen offers simulated signals, labelled as such everywhere.

The tower is my October project, phraseology. Readback runs it unchanged, as a separate program on the same computer. Everything that reacts to the camera is new.

How It Responds to Human Signals

Readback asks the SDK for three signals, and nothing else:

Signal What the SDK gives What Readback does with it
Pulse rate an average over 12 seconds your reference, the live difference, and the climb after each message
Breathing rate an average over 30 seconds your reference during the calm minute
Chest movement the breathing waveform breaths counted while you listen, and the breathing guide

The wiring is the SDK's renderer entry point, with telemetry off:

const sdk = new SmartSpectraSDK({
  apiKey,  // read by the main process from a file in your home folder
  requestedMetrics: [MetricType.CHEST_BREATHING, MetricType.BREATHING_RATE, MetricType.PULSE_RATE],
  enableTelemetry: false,
});
sdk.on('metrics', (buf) => store.add(decodeMetrics(buf)));
sdk.on('validationStatus', (code) => showHint(code)); // "face the camera", "more light"…
await sdk.start(); // only after the consent screen

The most useful page was Presage's model card. It says the breathing rate doesn't hold while the person is talking. But a radio exchange is talking, a few seconds of listening, and talking again. There are never 30 quiet seconds.

So I used the chest movement instead, which the SDK streams next to the rate. Readback takes the moments when you are listening, removes the slow drift, and counts the breaths. The same count on the calm minute gives the reference. It's a rough count, but it's enough to notice that you breathe faster than at rest. Readback never shows a breathing number while you talk.

When that count is up by 4 breaths a minute or more, the breathing guide opens. You can change that threshold, or turn the guide off. It breathes four seconds in and six out, three times, and draws your own chest moving under the circle. The space bar skips it.

The timeline needed one correction. My first version ranked the messages by how high the pulse went above the calm minute. On the first test, with simulated signals, every message after a "negative" looked stressful, because the pulse was still up. Now a message's climb starts from the pulse at its first word. The level against the calm minute sits next to it.

Here is the timeline after my own circuit:

The clearance to land came first, with a climb of 14 beats per minute. The take-off clearance came third. Between them, the tower's request to read back the vacate instruction, which came right after landing, while my pulse was still up. Before both clearances, the breathing guide opened, and both times I skipped it to read back.

HRV and facial expressions are left out on purpose. HRV needs a full minute, longer than an exchange. And a label like "fear" on someone learning would be a judgement, with nothing true to add to the practice.

Prize Categories

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use. Radio nerves are part of learning to fly, and the usual advice is "practise more", with nobody to practise with. Readback gives you a tower to practise with, and a mirror of what it does to you. The design follows from consent and from the SDK's limits: the camera opens only after you agree, the preview is blurred by default, the numbers are differences from your own calm minute, breathing is read only while you listen, and nothing is saved unless you ask.

Most Creative or Delightful Use. The signal changes the conversation, not just a dashboard. When your breathing has picked up, the tower waits for you, and you watch your own chest move under the breathing circle. The tower's voice goes through a small radio filter with a squelch, and the screens use B612, the typeface designed for cockpit displays.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Consent first. The first screen says what is measured, what stays on the computer, what goes to Presage and how to stop. The camera opens only after "I agree, turn the camera on". The microphone is a separate choice; without it, you type your readbacks. Until you agree, the app refuses every camera and microphone request.
  • Visible and stoppable. "Camera on" and "Stop camera" stay at the top while the camera runs. Closing the window stops everything, and the camera turns off at the end of each circuit.
  • Images: never recorded, saved or sent by Readback.
  • Your voice: kept in memory while you hold the key, transcribed on the same computer by the tower, then dropped. Never written to disk.
  • Measurements: in memory during the session. Saved only if you press "Save on this computer", as a small file with your reference, the tower's messages, whether each readback was accepted, and the climbs. No image, no audio, no transcript. One button deletes every saved session.
  • What goes to Presage: the SDK computes pulse and breathing on the computer. It contacts Presage's service to check the API key and the plan. The SDK's usage telemetry is on by default; Readback turns it off.
  • No AI service. No language model writes anything about you. The tower's readback checks are plain rules.
  • Nothing else leaves the computer. The app's page can't reach the network. Setup downloads the packages and the speech models once; after that, the tower runs offline.

I built Readback to practise the long readbacks. My pulse cared about two short sentences.

Pilots: which radio call still gets you, years after the licence?

articles.title: I made my app's 2-minute launch film entirely in code
articles.description: My app, Orbit OS, needed a film: two minutes that show every feature of a TV home screen and walk...
articles.body_html:
My app, Orbit OS, needed a film: two minutes that show every feature of a TV home screen and walk through the whole setup. I don't use editing software, so my AI pair programmer and I wrote the film instead.

Here's how it works, and why I'd do it this way again.

Every frame is a function of time

The film is one HTML page. It has the TV, the phone, the captions and the setup guide as plain DOM, and one function:

function seek(t) { apply(compute(t), t); }

compute(t) builds a state object for the time t: where the TV sits, which screen layer is visible, where the home row's focus is, which phone screenshot is showing, how far each caption has risen. apply() writes that state onto the DOM. Nothing animates by itself: there are no CSS transitions and no requestAnimationFrame. The same t always gives the same frame.

That one rule makes everything else easy. A scene is just a time range:

if (t >= 31.2 && t < 40.8) { // Live TV
  S.L.live = t >= 31.75 ? 1 : 0;
  S.live.open = E.out5(lin(t, 31.75, 32.3));   // the card opens into the picture
  S.live.guide = win(t, 33.0, 36.5, 0.35, 0.35); // the guide slides in, then out
  if (t >= 35.4) { S.live.ch = [19, 'Aastha']; S.live.zap = t - 35.4; }
}

The "launcher" in the film is the real one's design rebuilt in DOM: a row of cards on the inside of a cylinder (translate3d plus rotateY from the card's distance to the focus), a glow that takes the focused app's colour, and a streak of light across the focused card. The phone screens are real screenshots of the app, captured with Playwright from its own demo mode.

Rendering: Playwright as a frame grabber 

for (let f = first; f <= last; f++) {
  await page.evaluate((t) => window.seek(t), f / FPS);
  await page.screenshot({ path: `frames/f${String(f).padStart(5, '0')}.jpg`, type: 'jpeg', quality: 95 });
}

Six pages render in parallel. At 1080p and 30 fps the 4,050 frames take about 45 seconds on a laptop. With deviceScaleFactor: 2 the same page renders at 4K, and at 60 fps that's 8,100 frames for the final version. ffmpeg joins them with the sound.

One gotcha: anything random has to be random per frame, not per call, or a re-render changes the picture. The TV static uses a hash of the time instead of Math.random().

The music is code too

No stock music and no samples: score.py writes the soundtrack with numpy, on the same cue list as the picture. Plucked notes are Karplus-Strong strings. The bells use FM synthesis. Pads are detuned saws through a spectral low-pass. Every UI click in the film has a tick at the same timestamp. A noise-burst reverb glues it together, a sidechain makes the pad breathe with the kick, and a two-pass loudnorm brings it to -14 LUFS for YouTube and X.

def pluck(f, dur=0.5, level=0.18):
    P = int(SR / f)                      # one period of the string
    out = np.zeros(int(dur * SR) + P)
    out[:P] = rng.uniform(-1, 1, P)      # pluck: a burst of noise
    for i in range(P, len(out) - P, P):  # each period is the last one, averaged and damped
        prev = out[i - P:i]
        shifted = np.concatenate(([out[i - P - 1]], prev[:-1]))
        out[i:i + P] = 0.997 * 0.5 * (prev + shifted)
    ...

Why bother

  • Fixes are one line. "The phone covers the toast in step 3" became left: 510px, then a 45-second re-render.
  • The film can't drift from the app. The screens are the app's own, and the captions sit in an array next to their times.
  • It's reviewable. Every scene was checked by rendering stills at chosen times and looking at contact sheets, the same way you'd review a UI.

The source for Orbit OS is GPL-3.0 on GitHub, and the app is free on Google Play. If you've rendered video from code another way, I'd love to hear how.

Written with my AI assistant, from the film's real code.

articles.title: Systole - your heartbeat is the drum machine
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge What I Built Systole is a musical...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge
What I Built
Systole is a musical instrument that knows exactly one thing about you: what your body is doing right now.

You sit in front of a webcam, press Start, and it plays. Your heartbeat is the drummer - every systolic upstroke SmartSpectra finds in the arterial pressure waveform fires a kick drum and a ring of light, and the interval between your actual beats is the tempo of the piece. Your breathing opens the orchestra: as your chest rises a low-pass filter opens and the pad swells, and as you exhale it closes again. HRV picks the mode - open major pentatonic when you're calmer than your own session baseline, minor pentatonic when you're more charged. Pulse rate picks the key, and a smile adds a bell.

No wearable. No controller. No microphone. No "tap here to play". The interface is your autonomic nervous system.

The Systole instrument running: a glowing orb pulsing with the beat, a tempo readout of 73 bpm captioned "the kit is on your pulse", live pulse and breathing readouts, and the arterial pressure waveform along the bottom

That shot comes from a headless CI run on a machine with no camera, so the app badges
it SIMULATED - the demo video above is the real thing, with a real pulse in front of a
real lens.

The moment I was aiming for: you sit still, slightly bored, and then the kick lands on your own heartbeat. Not near it, not at a tempo somebody typed in - on the beat the SDK just heard in your face. People stop talking when that happens. Then they laugh, their pulse moves, and the music moves with it.

A single unbroken take, with the camera preview, the live pulse number and the music all on screen at once, so you can hear the tempo tracking the reading. Two moments worth watching for:

0:20-0:45 - the kick locks onto the detected beats. The caption under the big tempo readout switches from "tempo from pulse rate while the waveform settles" to "N beats heard in the pressure wave - the kit is on your pulse". That's the waveform driving it, not a reported average.
1:10 - I cover the lens for three seconds. Signal quality collapses, the pad closes down and the bells stop, because the app refuses to keep playing to a body it can no longer see. Uncovering brings it back.
There's also a landing page at SITE_URL describing the app, the signal mapping and the privacy design. Systole needs Electron and the native SmartSpectra runtime, so the page describes the instrument rather than running it - clone the repo to play.

Code
github.com/SarthakPatil18/Systole - MIT licensed, public, with setup instructions in the README.

Bash

git clone https://github.com/SarthakPatil18/Systole.git systole
cd systole
npm install
npm start # paste your Presage API key into the consent sheet
npm test # 18 logic tests + a headless run of the real renderer
Stack: Electron plus the renderer-side @smartspectra/node-sdk binding, esbuild for the renderer bundle, and hand-written Web Audio and Canvas 2D - no audio library, no charting library, no UI framework.

Three layers of tests, all runnable without a camera:

npm test - 18 logic tests (musical mapping, breath normalisation, beat detection including the dicrotic-notch regression below) plus a headless run that fakes the DOM, canvas and Web Audio and executes the actual bundled renderer.
npm run check:sdk - loads the real SDK native runtime, proves the metric list is accepted, and drives start() to the authentication boundary.
SYSTOLE_SCREENSHOT / SYSTOLE_SMOKE_JS - scriptable headless UI runs on a virtual display. Every screenshot in this post came out of one of those.
How It Responds to Human Signals
Systole requests [...breathingMetrics, ...cardioMetrics, MetricType.EXPRESSIONS] and uses four of the SDK's signals in genuinely different ways:

Signal What it does in the instrument
Arterial pressure trace Beat detection -> kick drum + light ring. Beat-to-beat interval is the tempo.
Chest + abdomen traces Normalised into a breath phase -> pad filter cutoff and gain. You hear yourself breathe.
HRV (Baevsky index) Compared to a slow baseline of your own session -> chooses the pentatonic mode.
Pulse rate Sets the root of the piece and covers the tempo while the waveform is still settling.
Expressions A smile raises the probability of a bell ornament. Optional - the app rebuilds without it if your plan doesn't include face metrics.
Validation status + confidence Fades the pad, suppresses new notes, shows the SDK's hint in plain language.
The integration is deliberately the boring, recommended one for Electron:

main.js
calls bindSmartSpectraIpc(win) and points webPreferences.preload at @smartspectra/node-sdk/preload. One SDK instance per window, torn down on close.
The renderer constructs SmartSpectraSDK from @smartspectra/node-sdk/renderer, so the SDK owns capture and hands back a MediaStream via streamAvailable for the preview. The microphone is never requested.
Metrics arrive as protobuf on the metrics event and are decoded with the SDK's own decodeMetrics from @smartspectra/node-sdk/messages.
If the plan rejects expression metrics (kConfigurationFailed / kMetricNotAuthorized), the app rebuilds without them and says so instead of dying.
Then the interesting part.

  1. Beats, not averages. The SDK gives a waveform, not beat events, so
    signal-engine.js
    finds the systolic upstroke itself: a sample has to clear the recent mean plus 35% of the swing and 72% of the recent peak-to-peak range, then fall back near the mean before it can re-arm. That amplitude gate is what stops the dicrotic notch counting as a second heartbeat - the bug that doubles your tempo. There's a regression test pinning it. The resulting intervals go through a 7-sample median, so one bad frame can't rewrite the groove, and the median interval is the tempo.

  2. Breath as a continuous control. Chest and abdomen traces are normalised against an 8-second rolling min/max into a breathPhase (0 = exhaled, 1 = inhaled), smoothed, and mapped to filter cutoff and pad gain. You can hear yourself breathe within two seconds, long before the 30-second breathing-rate window completes.

  3. HRV relative to you. Baevsky's stress index only means something against a personal baseline, so the app builds one from your own session (a slow 2% EMA) and compares against it. Crossing +25% of baseline shifts the mode darker; sitting 15% under it opens the bright one. Nobody's absolute number decides anything.

  4. Quality is audible. A quality value from the SDK's confidence scores and validationStatus control pad brightness and volume and suppress new notes. Bad light, motion, or no face means a thinner, quieter piece, with the SDK's validation hint shown as plain language ("Too dark - face a window or a lamp"). The instrument degrades honestly instead of inventing a reading.

Everything is scheduled with Web Audio lookahead (25 ms tick, 120 ms ahead) so the music never stutters when a frame is slow, and the audio graph is built once and retuned rather than reallocated on chord changes.

Prize Categories
Entering both - the honest fit is somewhere in between.

Most Creative or Delightful Use. The thing that made me build it: a pulse is something you cannot perceive without a device touching you, and music is the one medium where "here is what your body is doing" needs no explanation. Your heart becomes a drummer - not a visualisation of a drummer, an actual one, playing in time with you. The delight is realising the room is being kept in time by your own body, and the fact that the same ninety seconds makes people lean in, go quiet, then start tapping.

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use. What I removed on purpose points at who this is for. There is no wearable and no hands - nothing to strap on, hold, tap or charge - so the instrument is playable by people who can't grip a controller, who can't wear something on their wrist, or find both sensory-hostile, and by anyone who simply won't wear a heart-rate sensor. It also shows the signal without interpreting it: no scores, no stress level, no "you seem anxious", no diagnosis. For someone prone to over-monitoring their own body, "listen to this and breathe" is a kinder interface than a number that judges them. And because the mapping only ever nudges between gentle pentatonic modes, nothing the app detects can produce an alarming sound - the worst case of a wild reading is slightly odd music, which is the right failure mode for a wellness toy.

Consent and Data Handling
Full detail in PRIVACY.md; the summary:

Consent gate. Nothing touches the camera until the person has read a plain-language sheet, ticked an explicit consent checkbox ("my camera will be used to measure my pulse and breathing while Systole is running") and pressed Begin. The tick is per-session and is not stored - the next launch asks again.

The consent sheet: what the camera is used for, that nothing is recorded, the API key field, an opt-in diagnostics checkbox and the required consent checkbox

In
main.js
the camera is granted only for a video-only permission request, only from the app's own bundled file:// page; audio requests and any non-local origin are denied. Navigation and popups are blocked so the window can't be steered somewhere else. macOS's own prompt and camera indicator stay in force, and Stop releases the camera immediately.

Processing. Frames go from the renderer to the SmartSpectra SDK in the app's main process; measurement is on-device. Systole itself records nothing: no video, no audio, no vitals history, no session log, no analytics, no account, no identifiers. The API key is held in memory for the session and never written to disk; it is sent only to Presage's authenticated API.

Network. The only traffic Systole causes is the SDK's API-key authentication and subscription check - no video and no measured values in that request. There is no cloud service, no LLM call, and no optional AI feature in this app.

SDK telemetry - reversed default, disclosed. Presage's SDK telemetry is on by default; Systole sets enableTelemetry from an unchecked box on the consent sheet, so it is off unless the person opts in. If enabled, the SDK sends aggregate measurement-session summaries (SDK build, platform/device/arch, session shape, throughput and startup timings, counts of quality warnings, coarse error codes, a timestamp) and full device-readiness diagnostic reports - no raw frames and no measured physiological values. Those requests are authenticated, so they can be correlated with an account and shouldn't be called anonymous. Readiness reports live in Presage's private diagnostic storage with no automatic expiry; deletion follows Presage's policies. Turning it off means the SDK starts no telemetry session at all.

Retention and deletion. There is nothing to retain: quit the app and the session is gone, no server-side copy of measurements exists, and no files are written. For Presage-side diagnostic records, contact support@presagetech.com.

Not a medical device. Pulse, breathing, HRV and expression signals are used here for wellness and entertainment. Systole makes no diagnosis or treatment claims, takes no medical decisions, has no alerting or emergency behaviour, and is not for covert or non-consensual monitoring - it measures only the person who consented, in front of their own camera, with a visible indicator, and it never runs hidden or in the background. The consent sheet and the side rail both say so, inside the app, not just here.

articles.body_html:
Whenever I had a spare moment, I built small samples of interactions I wanted to try, the way you jot ideas down in a notebook. None of them made it into a real product, so I gave them a room of their own.

Interaction Library is a small room drawn in Three.js. Every notebook on the shelf holds one sample. Point at one and a live preview rises above the shelf. Click, and the notebook comes out, turns to face you and opens, with the sample already running on its right-hand page. Click the page and the sample fills the screen.

There are eleven samples so far, each named for one movement of the hand, like Drag, Skew, Zoom, Throw and Strum. The photos in them are my own, from everyday life. The room has a few small things of its own too. The lamp has a pull cord, the window's sky follows your local time, and the clock on the bookcase keeps the real time.

 

Three things I learned building it

Let the parts of a movement overlap. My first version opened a notebook in steps. Pull it out, turn it, open the cover. It looked mechanical. Now each part has a window inside one 1.6-second move, and the windows overlap, so nothing waits its turn.

// windows as shares of one 1.6 s move, shelf to open spread
const OUT = { tip: [0, 0.34], turn: [0.2, 0.9], open: [0.28, 1] };

// p runs from 0 to 1 over the move
const win = ([a, b]) => easeInOut(clamp((p - a) / (b - a), 0, 1));

book.quaternion.slerpQuaternions(onShelf, facingYou, win(OUT.turn));
cover.rotation.y = -openAngle * win(OUT.open);

 

Keep the frame of the click light. Opening a notebook writes both of its pages into canvas textures. Uploading them in the frame of the click took about 5 ms, or 12 ms at a larger size, a big share of one frame. Now they wait in a queue and go to the GPU one per frame.

// in the render loop
if (queue.length) renderer.initTexture(queue.shift());

 
A WebGL page can still be a web page. Arrow keys move along the shelf, Enter opens a notebook and Esc steps back. prefers-reduced-motion stills the idle movement, and the page carries a plain HTML version with real links for screen readers and search engines. Lighthouse gives it 100 for accessibility, best practices and SEO, on desktop and on phones.

 

Stack

Three.js for the room and five of the samples, Canvas 2D for five more, and DOM transforms with GSAP for Drag, all in plain JavaScript. Phones get a lighter room with a smaller shadow map, and a sample is only built when its notebook is touched.

Try it at library.jjangik.kr.

Which one feels best under your hand? I'd love to hear.
